articles.title: Saudi-led anti-Houthi coalition downs drone headed toward Mecca
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis said it intercepted a drone over the Mecca region following a series of attacks by the Iran-backed militants against the kingdom. "Inter...
articles.full_text:
The Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis said it intercepted a drone over the Mecca region following a series of attacks by the Iran-backed militants against the kingdom.
"Interception and destruction of a drone in the Mecca region," Turki al-Malki, the coalition's spokesperson wrote on social media, without elaborating on the source of the attack.
The interception came a day after the coalition said that it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile and two drones fired by the Houthis toward Saudi territory.
Mecca is home to one of Islam's holiest sites, the Kabba, which draws millions of pilgrims every year, making it a red line for Saudi Arabia and the Muslim world in general.
The development follows escalating hostilities between the Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition, which supports Yemen's internationally recognized government.
Earlier Tuesday, the Houthis claimed that Saudi strikes had killed 17 civilians over two days this week.
The Houthi Health Ministry said in a statement that most of the people killed were children, "which shows that Saudi aircraft are targeting homes, residential neighborhoods and markets."
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said Monday evening that Riyadh had carried out "109 strikes over the past 24 hours" in Yemen, targeting the governorates of Saada, Taiz, Lahj, al-Jawf and Hodeidah.
The group also claimed drone attacks on Saudi airports in the east and south of the kingdom.
Yemen has been beset by war since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, with a Saudi-led coalition entering the conflict a year later in support of the government.
A 2022 truce fell apart in July and, in September, the Houthis launched an offensive to capture the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which links Europe to Asia via the Red Sea and Suez Canal.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country.

articles.title: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine - CNN
articles.summary: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine  CNNWorld leaders who sparred with Trump express relief mixed with caution at Republican election rout  AP NewsDemocrats seize control of Congress: How are the US and the world reacting?  CGTNWhat Trump losing power over Congress means for Iran, Ukraine and foreign policy  CNBCWhat Trump’s Midterm Defeat Means for Iran and Oil Prices  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
The US midterm elections could have consequences far beyond the country’s borders. President Donald Trump has spent nearly two years overturning decades of American foreign policy, unsettling allies and adversaries alike. Now, both are watching to see how an electoral setback at home will shape his actions abroad.
For Iran, Israel and Ukraine, the stakes go well beyond who controls Congress. The result could influence whether Trump pursues a deal with Tehran or more war, how much Washington’s longstanding support for Israel erodes, and how hard he pushes Kyiv to accept terms to end Russia’s war.
Democrats will have new tools to challenge Trump. But he still has considerable freedom to act abroad, leaving world leaders with a question: Will defeat make him more willing to compromise, or more determined to get his way?
Here’s how the vote could impact Washington’s most pressing foreign policy concerns:
Iran gloats, but gets no guarantee of peace
Iran is celebrating Trump’s midterm setback, but it is bracing for what comes next: a possible new US strike or a fresh push for a deal.
Trump admitted in a call with Fox News that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans’ losses but Vice President JD Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.”
After eight months of striking the region’s economic lifelines to turn American voters against the war, Tehran has hailed the Republican loss as a public verdict on it. Trump acknowledged that war-driven price hikes played a role.
“If the US government betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has led negotiations with the US, wrote on X.
Tehran is not betting on a change of course in Washington. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said anyone who believes the results will shift US policy is “deeply mistaken,” and officials say Iran’s strategy doesn’t hinge on American elections as they prepare for more war while intensifying diplomacy.
The risk of escalation is real. Reports that Trump might order new, more intense strikes are fueling anxiety across the region, and Tehran has warned that its retaliation would be much wider in scope than in earlier rounds. This week, Trump told some journalists he is considering striking Iran hard, and others that he has no immediate plans to escalate.
“The Iran war has become a political albatross around his neck, leaving (Trump) with a stark choice: cut a face-saving deal and declare victory, or double down militarily to reclaim the initiative,” Ali Vaez of International Crisis Group told CNN. “The danger is that a president weakened at the ballot box may seek redemption on the battlefield.”
Diplomacy offers another path. Talks that stagnated over the summer have picked up in the past week, with Tehran sending officials to Qatari mediators who are circulating proposals with Washington. Before the vote, Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Trump agreed to its seven conditions.
Sanam Vakil of Chatham House said Iran’s leadership “might feel vindicated,” but that “does not necessarily solve their problems.” Trump needs a diplomatic victory yet may be reluctant to appear weak, she said, while Tehran could read his setback as a chance to demand greater concessions. She expects intensified diplomacy alongside military threats, with an interim Strait of Hormuz deal “more realistic” than a comprehensive one.
‘End of an era’ for US-Israel relations
In Israel, the election day announcement that Trump would abruptly cut off US military aid to the country was the first surprise. The results, with Democrats sweeping both chambers of Congress in what has been called a “blue tsunami,” are a five-alarm fire in Israel.
Bipartisan support for Israel in the US had already been eroding, with Democrats outraged at Israel over the death toll in the Gaza war and a growing number of Republicans believing the US has given it too much support.
“The only bipartisan issue right now is criticism of Israel,” said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to the US. “It’s an organizing principle for the Democratic Party,” he told CNN. “And it’s becoming an organizing principle for much of the Republican Party.”
Oren said the end of US aid is just the beginning of a process that has only started to play out. He said it’s conceivable that the US could end intelligence sharing with Israel and the joint development of critical military systems, such as the vaunted Iron Dome aerial defense system. He also pointed to the United Nations Security Council, where Republican and Democratic presidents have protected Israel with the US veto.
“We are at the end of an era,” he said.
Yaakov Katz, a former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, warned there is more to come. “What Trump announced about the military aid yesterday is just the tip of the iceberg of what can change – arms sales could be blocked, sanctions will be proposed and joint economic programs defunded,” he said on X.
The anti-Israel sentiment only hardened during the Iran war, with segments of the US electorate viewing the joint US-Israel strikes as a war that Netanyahu sold to Trump. Even now, Netanyahu has been pushing to resume strikes on Iran, which would reignite a war that drove gas prices and the cost of living higher and contributed to Republicans’ devastating midterm performance.
Netanyahu also faces turmoil at home. In elections a week before the midterms, he lost his majority in parliament, but his main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, does not have an outright majority and would likely need to cooperate with Arab parties, who saw record turnout.
Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, warned that Israel “does not have time to waste” in replacing Netanyahu and leading the country away from sanctions and isolation.
Ukraine waits for a post-Trump world
For Kyiv, the reaction came before the election. And on Wednesday there was relative silence.
For weeks, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s relationship with Trump has been in freefall. Trump has demanded Zelensky be replaced; courted energy deals to benefit Russia; and watched as Ukraine’s tech and intel dependencies on the US were inexplicably thwarted. And so Kyiv was forced to take a position early: wait, with urgency, for a post-Trump world.
And when it began to dawn on Wednesday, there was little official comment from Kyiv, Zelensky perhaps happy for the memes of him, sat with a beer and popcorn in front of the mid-term TV coverage, to do the job for him.
A deputy in his office, Sergiy Kyslytsia, pledged on Ukrainian TV that the country would continue to “develop genuine, normal and stable relations” with whoever is in office, seek Patriot interceptors, and navigate both a new Congress and the likely flurry of executive orders that may try to obviate it.
But there can be no disguising that a crestfallen Trump, and the slow clock now loudly ticking on his worldview and presidency, is in Kyiv’s favour. He had claimed a peace was easy to fashion, yet proceeded to punish Ukraine for not agreeing to the demands of its invader. He humiliated, scolded, and then occasionally made up with, Zelensky, while massaged by European allies, aghast at the breakdown in decades of security alliances.
There is still a lot that Ukraine needs Trump and the United States to do. Provide arms, money, and a wider assurance it is on their side. But Kyiv has calculated it cannot depend on Washington, after months of hostility.
There is one downside of the ticking clock however: that Russian President Vladimir Putin determines he has likely a year to pursue, at any cost, the best outcome possible in his war of choice, before the 2028 fight drags Republican policy back to the pro-Ukrainian mainstream. Putin has so far failed to use his apparent great ally, Trump, to secure a battlefield win of note. He may seek to change that while the embers of Trump’s authority burn.

articles.title: Iran Says Four Oil Tankers Destroyed by Mines Near Strait of Hormuz - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.summary: Iran Says Four Oil Tankers Destroyed by Mines Near Strait of Hormuz  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comIran's IRGC says two tankers and tugboat caught fire in Strait of Hormuz  ReutersIRGC: 2 tankers, tugboat attempting to use unauthorized Hormuz routes catch fire  The Times of IsraelIran Turns to Guerrilla Tactics in Bid to Reassert Grip on Strait of Hormuz  WSJFour oil tankers destroyed in Hormuz after hitting mines, Tehran says  France 24
articles.full_text:
Four oil tankers were destroyed after hitting naval mines in an area south of the Strait of Hormuz proscribed by Iran as prohibited for navigation, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday, as attacks on vessels in the region intensify while crude oil flows have dipped from recent highs.
The four tankers are still ablaze, while two other vessels have been seized, the Revolutionary Guards said.
While flows have recovered substantially from the lows in the spring, the security situation in and near the Strait of Hormuz has actually deteriorated, with a higher number of attacks on tankers in recent weeks.
Following a post-war peak in September, exports of crude oil, condensate, and fuels from the Middle East slipped to 17.1 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, down from 18.9 million bpd in September, according to data from Vortexa cited by Reuters.
“October data shows Middle East seaborne oil exports have pulled back slightly from recent post-war highs on heightened risks in the Strait of Hormuz,” George Morris, an analyst at Vortexa, said in comments reported by the publication.
Kpler has tracked a 1-million-bpd drop in total crude oil and condensate exports. Crude and condensate flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Oman are estimated, provisionally, to have dropped to 16.1 million bpd in October, from 17.09 million bpd in September.
However, the tanker-tracking services caution that the numbers could be revised up as more details on shipments, especially shuttle shipments, emerge in the coming days.
Oil flows from the Middle East region have materially increased since the lows in April and May, but the heightened security concerns and intensified attacks, mines, and other explosions and incidents are making tracking shipments difficult. Tanker-trackers increasingly rely on satellite imagery to confirm movements because vessels are often switching off transponders to avoid detection when transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Israeli claims of Iran chemical weapons threat divide US officials
articles.summary: Israeli intelligence allegations that Iran may be preparing to use chemical weapons against its adversaries have sparked debate within the U.S. administration, with officials quest...
articles.full_text:
Israeli intelligence allegations that Iran may be preparing to use chemical weapons against its adversaries have sparked debate within the U.S. administration, with officials questioning both the reliability of the claims and Israel's intentions in raising the alarm, The New York Times reported Tuesday.
Some U.S. officials reportedly view the claims as part of an effort by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government to persuade the administration of President Donald Trump to resume large-scale military operations against Iran.
Others argue that the warnings should be taken seriously amid growing concerns over Tehran’s potential attacks on American interests.
The concerns have also been shared with Gulf countries. However, a regional official told the Times that Israeli officials presented assessments suggesting Iran was working to make its chemical weapons operational without providing supporting evidence. Gulf governments reportedly found the claims unconvincing.
For some American officials, the allegations have revived memories of the flawed U.S. intelligence assessments in 2002 that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, claims used to justify the 2003 invasion.
While U.S. intelligence agencies have long monitored Iran’s chemical weapons capabilities, the report said officials remain divided over whether Tehran has the capacity to deploy such weapons effectively or would ever choose to use them.
Iran has repeatedly denied possessing chemical weapons, previously dismissing such accusations as part of an Israeli psychological warfare campaign.
The intelligence dispute comes as Washington and Tehran explore diplomatic options to prevent renewed fighting, while U.S. forces continue building up their military presence in the region, the report said.
The report noted that the U.S. military is preparing for possible renewed strikes on Iran as early as Wednesday, pending authorization by President Donald Trump.

articles.title: Iran claims 4 tankers destroyed in Hormuz after hitting naval mines
articles.summary: Iran claimed Wednesday at least four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, following a warning that no one would benefit from a return to war. It cam...
articles.full_text:
Iran claimed Wednesday at least four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, following a warning that no one would benefit from a return to war.
It came a day after President Donald Trump said the United States had launched strikes on the Islamic republic, following reports of a raid on Qeshm, the largest island in the strait.
"Four non-compliant oil tankers attempting to pass through the prohibited passage south of the Strait of Hormuz were destroyed after striking naval mines and are still burning," Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement quoted by state TV.
"Two other non-compliant ships or vessels have also been halted," it added.
The Guards also said they had shot down a drone over the strait.
Tehran claims control over Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, and has targeted vessels that attempt to cross without its authorization since the war erupted.
The conflict, triggered by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, has been at a stalemate for months.
Indirect contact between the United States and Iran via mediators has continued with little sign of any diplomatic breakthrough and Iran has said it is ready to reopen the strait but only if Washington agrees to a long-standing list of demands.
Tehran's chief negotiator in talks with the United States, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Islamic republic was "ready for battle with its finger on the trigger," although President Masoud Pezeshkian insisted his government was trying to resolve the crisis "through dialogue."
"No one will benefit from this war" if fighting resumes, Pezeshkian said Tuesday.

The future of investment is no longer shaped by capital alone. It is increasingly shaped by strategic partnerships, policy credibility, and countries' ability to connect opportunity with confidence.
Ghana’s engagement with Saudi Arabia’s investment community in Riyadh reflects a deliberate economic diplomacy strategy to translate national development priorities into international investment partnerships.
An investment webinar organised by the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority (GIPA), in collaboration with the Embassy of Ghana in Riyadh, provided a platform to present Ghana’s economic opportunities, investment reforms and development priorities to prospective investors in the Kingdom.
Held under the theme, “Ghana is Open for Business: Unlocking Opportunities for Investors,” the engagement formed part of GIPA’s broader mandate to promote Ghana as a competitive investment destination and facilitate partnerships that support economic transformation.
The initiative is aligned with the strategic direction of GIPA’s Chief Executive Officer, Simon Madjie, whose leadership has emphasised stronger international investor engagement, closer collaboration with Ghana’s diplomatic missions and the attraction of investments that create jobs, strengthen industries and accelerate value creation.
Investment promotion as an economic strategy
In the modern global economy, investment promotion has moved beyond the attraction of financial resources. Countries increasingly seek investments that contribute to productivity, technology transfer, export competitiveness and sustainable development.
Ghana’s approach reflects this broader understanding.
Through the Regional and Global Operations Division (RGOD), GIPA is leveraging Ghana’s diplomatic network as a bridge between international investors and opportunities within the Ghanaian economy.
At the Riyadh engagement, Victoria Cobbah, Head of the RGOD, highlighted Ghana’s democratic stability, predictable regulatory environment and investor protection framework as key factors supporting business confidence. She also drew attention to Ghana’s strategic position as host of the Secretariat of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), providing investors with access to a continental market of more than 1.4 billion people.
For Saudi investors, this presents an opportunity to use Ghana not only as a destination market, but also as a base for accessing wider African markets.
Aligning Ghana’s priorities with Saudi vision 2030
The engagement also revealed significant areas of policy alignment between Ghana’s development agenda and Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030. Both countries are pursuing economic diversification, private-sector growth, infrastructure expansion, renewable energy development and technological advancement.
This alignment creates opportunities for partnerships in agriculture, manufacturing, logistics, energy, healthcare, tourism and digital services. Ghana’s investment proposition is increasingly centred on sectors capable of generating economic value beyond traditional commodity exports.
Government interventions supporting growth
Ghana’s investment drive is reinforced by government initiatives designed to address structural challenges and create a stronger environment for private enterprise.
The Big Push Programme represents government’s commitment to expanding infrastructure, particularly roads, transport networks and productive assets needed to improve business efficiency.
In agriculture, the Agriculture for Economic Transformation Agenda seeks to reposition the sector through commercialisation, mechanisation, irrigation and agro-processing. The objective is to create stronger agricultural value chains in which investors can participate in production, processing, storage and export.
The Digital Jobs Initiative reflects Ghana’s commitment to preparing its young population for the digital economy by expanding technology skills and supporting innovation-driven employment.
Meanwhile, initiatives such as the Black Star Experience and the Marine Drive Project demonstrate efforts to unlock investment opportunities in tourism, culture, hospitality and real estate.
Building investor confidence through dialogue
The interactive session provided Saudi businesses with an opportunity to explore practical issues affecting investment decisions.
Yusif Mustapha of the Regional and Global Operations Division addressed concerns relating to foreign ownership, investment protection and business establishment in Ghana. He explained that foreign investors can establish businesses in Ghana under applicable laws, including arrangements that permit full foreign ownership. He further highlighted the ability of investors to repatriate profits and dividends, reinforcing Ghana’s commitment to investor protection.
Participants also expressed interest in improved aviation connectivity between Ghana and Saudi Arabia, as well as developments in transport infrastructure. Discussions on projects such as the Volta Economic Corridor highlighted Ghana’s ambition to strengthen regional connectivity and improve trade facilitation.
Diplomacy supporting investment
The participation of Alhaji Said Sinare, Ambassador of Ghana to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, demonstrated the growing importance of economic diplomacy in strengthening commercial relations.
The Ambassador encouraged Saudi investors to explore opportunities in Ghana’s minerals, agriculture, energy and manufacturing sectors, while reaffirming the Embassy’s readiness to support investors.
The Riyadh engagement ultimately reinforced a central message: Ghana’s investment strategy is not simply about attracting capital; it is about building partnerships that support shared economic progress.
Ghana Investment Promotion Authority equips global missions to champion economic growth
In a world where countries compete not only for markets but also for investment, diplomacy is taking on a new economic role. Foreign missions are increasingly becoming bridges between national ambitions and global investors seeking stable, credible and high-growth destinations.
Ghana is embracing this shift by empowering its diplomatic missions with the knowledge and tools needed to promote the country’s investment opportunities more effectively.
As part of this strategy, GIPA, under the leadership of Chief Executive Officer Simon Madjie, is strengthening collaboration with Ghana’s missions abroad to position the country as a preferred destination for sustainable investment.
This vision was demonstrated through a capacity-building webinar organised for officials of the Ghana Mission in Brussels, aimed at enhancing their understanding of Ghana’s economic landscape, government priorities and emerging investment opportunities.
Connecting policy with investment opportunities
The session was led by Ms Victoria Cobbah, Head of the Regional and Global Operations Division (RGOD) at GIPA, who provided insights into Ghana’s economic agenda, investment initiatives, competitive advantages and incentives available to investors.
The engagement highlighted government’s commitment to building a resilient and competitive economy anchored on macroeconomic stability, industrial growth, productivity and private-sector participation.
Key policy initiatives presented included the Big Push Agenda, which seeks to accelerate infrastructure development and improve economic connectivity; the 24-Hour Economy Programme, designed to increase productivity and create new employment opportunities; and the Volta Economic Corridor Project, which aims to unlock economic potential through improved transport, agriculture and industrial development.
Other strategic programmes highlighted included the Goldbod initiative, the Agro-Ecological Parks Programme, the Sahel Cargo Hub Strategy and the Import Substitution Industrialisation Programme.
Together, these initiatives demonstrate Ghana’s ambition to move beyond raw commodity exports towards a value-driven economy in which investors can participate in manufacturing, processing, innovation and job creation.
Ghana’s investment advantage
Ghana’s investment proposition is built on stability, opportunity and access.
The webinar highlighted the country’s democratic credentials, peaceful business environment, strategic location and growing consumer market as key factors supporting investor confidence.
Ghana’s role as host of the AfCFTA Secretariat was also emphasised as a major advantage, providing investors with a gateway to Africa’s expanding single market.
The country’s improving infrastructure, growing digital economy and investment incentives, including Free Zones benefits and sector-specific incentives, further strengthen Ghana’s competitiveness.
Brussels mission explores strategic sectors
For Ambassador Henry Tachie-Menson, Ghana’s Ambassador to Belgium, the engagement provided an opportunity to deepen the Mission’s understanding of priority sectors and strengthen its ability to engage potential investors.
The discussions focused on areas with strong investment potential, including renewable energy, critical minerals, cocoa, agriculture, technology, real estate, mining infrastructure and AfCFTA-related opportunities.
In energy, attention was drawn to opportunities in solar power, hydrogen development, lithium processing and sustainable energy solutions.

articles.title: Middle East weekly: Dubai Chambers launches AI marketplace, Saudi Arabia approves commercial law, Invest Qatar wins UN award, and more - KrASIA
articles.summary: Middle East weekly: Dubai Chambers launches AI marketplace, Saudi Arabia approves commercial law, Invest Qatar wins UN award, and more  KrASIA
articles.full_text:
Chinese companies expand in the Middle East
JD Property adds warehouse in Dubai’s Jebel Ali Free Zone
JD Property has added a high-specification logistics warehouse in Dubai’s Jebel Ali Free Zone, according to Guandian. It secured tenants before completing the acquisition, bringing the warehouse to full occupancy at handover.
The facility offers direct access to Jebel Ali Port and connections to major regional highways, supporting warehousing, distribution, cargo consolidation, and cross-border trade. The acquisition expands JD Property’s warehouse portfolio at a key Middle Eastern logistics hub, allowing it to serve businesses of different sizes.
FAW Jiefang ships first 210 trucks to the UAE
FAW Jiefang has shipped its first batch of 210 trucks to the UAE, marking its first sales in the market as it moved from building distribution channels and preparing products to bulk deliveries, Securities Daily reported.
The company has partnered with a major local automotive dealership group. Its distributor is developing sales, after-sales service, and spare parts networks. FAW Jiefang has also developed more than 10 models tailored to local transport requirements and regulations, including tractor units, cargo trucks, dump trucks, and concrete mixers.
Rox delivers first 100 UAE-made SUVs
Rox has announced the delivery of its first 100 luxury SUVs manufactured in the UAE, each bearing the “Made in the Emirates” mark, according to the Emirates News Agency. The deliveries mark a new stage in its production operations in Abu Dhabi.
The vehicles were produced at its artificial intelligence manufacturing center in Khalifa Economic Zones Abu Dhabi (KEZAD). The site combines a manufacturing center, AI laboratory, and design studio. The project aims to establish more of the company’s automotive manufacturing, design, AI, and R&D capabilities in the UAE.
Economic and policy developments
Dubai Chambers launches marketplace for business AI agents
Dubai Chambers has launched the “Chamber AI Hub,” describing it as the world’s first chamber-led marketplace for agentic AI. The platform gives Dubai businesses access to specialized AI agents designed to carry out administrative and operational tasks.
It currently offers 22 agents across seven functions: compliance, procurement, operations, finance, sales, human resources, and logistics. Dubai Chambers plans to expand the offering to 100 agents over the next two years as part of a program targeting more than 295,000 private businesses. Dubai Chambers will also provide specialized training for 14,000 companies in its business groups and councils to help them integrate AI agents into daily operations.
ADNOC identifies over AED 60 billion in UAE manufacturing opportunities
Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) has announced more than AED 60 billion (USD 16.3 billion) in domestic manufacturing opportunities through 2030, according to Arab News. These cover more than 200 products and a range of critical components, with the aim of replacing imports, shortening delivery times, and reducing exposure to global supply chain disruptions.
ADNOC plans to localize the manufacture of products worth AED 90 billion (USD 24.5 billion) by 2030. It also aims to channel AED 220 billion (USD 59.9 billion) into the UAE economy between 2025 and 2030 through its In-Country Value program.
Dubai Financial Market’s traded value rises 22%
The value of trading on Dubai Financial Market (DFM) rose 22% year-on-year to AED 162 billion (USD 44.1 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, Khaleej Times reported. Average daily traded value increased 25% to AED 883 million (USD 240.4 million), while the number of trades rose 24% to 3.16 million.
DFM added 55,460 investors during the period, 72% of whom were from overseas, bringing its total investor base to more than 1.3 million. Its market capitalization stood at approximately AED 993 billion (USD 270.4 billion) at the end of September.
UAE capital markets regulator reports 43% increase in licensed companies
The number of companies licensed by the UAE’s Capital Market Authority increased 43% YoY in the first nine months of 2026, while the number of licensed professionals rose 64%, according to authority data cited by Arab News.
The combined market capitalization of Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange and Dubai Financial Market reached AED 3.7 trillion (USD 1 trillion) at the end of September. Trading during the nine-month period totaled AED 408 billion (USD 111.1 billion), with foreign investors accounting for 49%.
Dubai AI Campus targets more than 1,000 companies by 2030
Dubai has raised its targets for the Dubai AI Campus, aiming to attract more than 1,000 AI companies and create over 5,000 highly skilled jobs by 2030.
The campus, located in Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), opened in May 2024 and now hosts more than 500 AI companies, reaching its original 2028 target two years early. Its companies have raised more than AED 1 billion (USD 272.3 million) from private equity and venture capital firms and created over 2,000 technology jobs.
ADIPEC expects record Asian delegation
The Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition and Conference (ADIPEC), taking place November 2 to 5, is welcoming its largest ever delegation from Asia this year, The National reported.
The Asian contingent comprises 353 companies and six national pavilions representing China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, and South Korea. Chinese exhibitors include Sinopec, China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC), China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC), and battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL).
Saudi cabinet approves new commercial law
Saudi Arabia’s cabinet approved a new law on commercial transactions that will broaden participation in business, including allowing Saudi citizens aged 15 and above to engage in commercial activities under specified conditions, Asharq Al-Awsat reported.
The law will replace three existing laws, strengthen fair competition and protections for small and medium-sized enterprises, clarify the rights and obligations of parties to commercial contracts, and recognize electronic documents as legal evidence.
Minors will need permission from a guardian, custodian, or court to trade. The law will take effect 180 days after publication in the official gazette.
Saudi winter tourism calendar spans nine destinations
Saudi Arabia has released its Saudi Winter events calendar, covering nine destinations including Riyadh, Medina, and the Red Sea, according to Saudi Gazette.
The program includes festivals, sporting events, live performances, heritage experiences, nature excursions, desert adventures, and leisure breaks, alongside dining, shopping, and coastal activities. The Saudi Tourism Authority brought together more than 100 public and private sector partners to develop the winter program, offering over 1,800 tourism products.
Saudi business sector revenue reaches SAR 5.628 trillion in 2025
Operating revenue in Saudi Arabia’s business sector increased 2.3% YoY to SAR 5.628 trillion (USD 1.5 trillion) in 2025, while employee compensation rose 6% to SAR 624.1 billion (USD 166.4 billion), according to General Authority for Statistics data cited by Saudi Gazette.
Electricity, gas, steam, and air conditioning supply recorded the fastest revenue growth, at 14.2%. Gross fixed capital formation in the business sector rose 0.4% to SAR 992 billion (USD 264.5 billion), with manufacturing accounting for the largest share of investment.
Saudi services exports rise 6.9% in 2025
Saudi Arabia’s services exports rose 6.9% in 2025 to SAR 251.7 billion (USD 67.1 billion), from SAR 235.5 billion (USD 62.8 billion) in 2024, according to General Authority for Statistics data reported by Saudi Gazette.
Travel services remained the largest export category at SAR 159.9 billion (USD 42.6 billion), followed by transport services at SAR 35.4 billion (USD 9.4 billion). Services imports increased 4.2% to SAR 488.6 billion (USD 130.3 billion).
Invest Qatar wins UN investment promotion award
Invest Qatar has received the 2026 United Nations Investment Promotion Award for its Startup Qatar initiative, recognizing its efforts to attract and support high-potential startups and technology companies, according to an official announcement.

articles.summary: Saudi Arabia oil revenues plunge 23% to 116.5 billion riyals in Q3 2026 as energy income weakens  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia has reported a sharp decline in oil revenues for the third quarter of 2026. Government oil income fell 23% year over year to 116.5 billion Saudi riyals, according to the latest figures shared by Saudi authorities.
The decline puts fresh attention on the kingdom's dependence on oil income. Despite efforts to diversify its economy, petroleum revenues remain an important source of government funding.
The latest figures also come at a challenging time for the Saudi energy sector. Regional conflict, lower oil production and disruptions to energy infrastructure have created additional pressure on the country's oil industry.
The 116.5 billion riyal figure represents government oil revenue. It should not be confused with Saudi Aramco's total sales or quarterly profits.
The decline is particularly important because Saudi Arabia continues to spend heavily on infrastructure, tourism, technology and other projects under its Vision 2030 economic transformation programme.
Saudi Arabia oil revenues fall 23% to 116.5 billion riyals
Saudi Arabia's government oil revenues dropped to 116.5 billion riyals in Q3 2026. This represents a 23% decline compared with the same quarter last year.
The latest figure highlights the pressure on the country's public finances as oil income weakens.
Oil revenue is important because it helps the Saudi government finance public services, infrastructure projects and large-scale development programmes.
A sustained decline can make it harder for the government to fund these commitments without relying more heavily on other sources of income.
Saudi Arabia has been trying to reduce its dependence on crude oil through Vision 2030. The programme aims to expand sectors such as tourism, entertainment, manufacturing, technology and financial services.
However, the latest revenue figures show that oil remains a major part of the country's economic structure.
The government is also dealing with changing conditions in the international energy market. Oil prices, production levels and export volumes can all influence how much money flows into its budget.
Saudi Arabia oil production faces pressure amid Middle East conflict
The revenue decline comes as Saudi Arabia faces challenges involving its oil production and energy infrastructure.
According to Reuters, Saudi oil production was around 8 million barrels per day in September 2026. This was down from slightly more than 10 million barrels per day before the US-Iran war.
The conflict has affected regional energy infrastructure and disrupted important shipping routes.
Saudi Arabia has also faced difficulties maintaining normal export operations. Its East-West Pipeline has become particularly important because it allows the kingdom to transport crude towards the Red Sea rather than relying entirely on shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
The country has been exploring additional overseas storage facilities and alternative export routes to protect its supply network.
These developments matter because higher oil prices do not automatically guarantee higher government revenue.
If production and export volumes fall significantly, the reduction in barrels sold can offset the benefit of stronger prices.
This creates a complicated situation for Saudi Arabia. The kingdom needs to maintain reliable exports while protecting its energy infrastructure from further disruptions.
Saudi Arabia Vision 2030 faces fresh oil revenue challenges
The decline in government oil income also raises questions about Saudi Arabia's economic diversification plans.
The kingdom has committed substantial resources to major projects involving tourism, entertainment, infrastructure and technology.
Vision 2030 is designed to create additional sources of economic growth and reduce the country's dependence on petroleum.
There are already signs of progress outside the energy sector. Saudi Arabia's non-oil economic activities grew 1.9% year over year in Q3 2026.
However, overall real GDP contracted 3.8% during the quarter. The decline was largely driven by a 20.4% contraction in oil activities.
This shows the difference between growth in non-oil industries and the wider economic impact of weaker oil production.
Saudi Aramco's latest financial results also provide an interesting contrast. The company reported adjusted net income of $31.2 billion for Q3 2026, compared with $28.6 billion a year earlier. Stronger realised crude prices and refining margins supported its performance.
However, Aramco's corporate earnings and the government's oil revenues measure different things. They should not be treated as interchangeable figures.
For Saudi Arabia, the challenge now is to protect oil exports while continuing to build alternative sources of income. The coming quarters will show whether non-oil growth can provide enough support to reduce the pressure created by weaker government oil receipts. The kingdom's ability to maintain its development spending while managing this revenue gap will be an important test for Vision 2030.

articles.title: Why Is Qatar Buying US LNG Despite Being a Global Gas Powerhouse? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Why Is Qatar Buying US LNG Despite Being a Global Gas Powerhouse?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
Qatar’s decision to secure long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the United States signals a significant shift in global energy markets. The world’s second-largest LNG exporter is increasingly looking beyond its own production capacity to protect itself against geopolitical instability in the Gulf, particularly the risks associated with the Strait of Hormuz.
QatarEnergy last week signed a 20-year agreement to purchase 3 million metric tons per year (mtpa) of LNG from Woodside Energy’s facilities in Louisiana. The deal followed earlier agreements with US producer Cheniere Energy for up to 4 mtpa from its Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi facilities through 2054.
Deliveries under the contracts are expected to begin in 2030 and 2031. Together, the agreements will make Qatar the largest buyer of US LNG.
QatarEnergy chief executive Saad al-Kaabi has also indicated that the company expects to sign further supply agreements with US and other international producers this year, potentially securing millions of tons of LNG from overseas sources for decades.
Qatar had already been expanding its international investments before the US-Iran war began on February 28. The state-owned energy company was acquiring stakes in LNG projects across North America and Africa to diversify its trading portfolio and improve its flexibility.
The latest agreements, however, reflect a deeper strategic calculation. Qatar is not simply expanding its international business. It is seeking protection against disruptions to its own exports by securing access to production facilities outside the Gulf.
The shift also highlights how the United States has emerged as a major beneficiary of changing perceptions of Middle Eastern energy security.
Bob McNally, founder and president of Rapidan Energy Group and a former White House energy adviser under President George W. Bush, recalled that US officials once worried about Washington becoming as dependent on Qatar for LNG as it was on OPEC for oil.
The shale revolution and the Iran war have dramatically changed that relationship. Qatar, once seen as a potential supplier on which the United States might depend, is now purchasing American gas.
US LNG becomes an insurance policy against Hormuz disruption
The Strait of Hormuz has become central to Qatar’s energy security calculations as Washington and Tehran continue to dispute the future of the strategic waterway.
Before the war, roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies passed through the strait. Its vulnerability has prompted Gulf producers to reconsider how they transport energy to international markets.
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are expanding or preparing to expand pipeline networks that allow them to export crude oil and refined fuels without relying entirely on Hormuz.
Qatar faces a considerably more difficult challenge because it has no viable alternative route for exporting LNG.
The country’s entire LNG industry is concentrated at the enormous Ras Laffan facility, where gas extracted from the North Field is processed before being shipped to customers worldwide. This concentration makes Qatar’s export capacity particularly vulnerable to disruptions in the Gulf.
The risks became clear in March, when an Iranian missile damaged two of QatarEnergy’s 14 LNG production trains at Ras Laffan. The damage removed approximately 17% of the country’s export capacity.
QatarEnergy estimated that the disruption would cost around $20 billion annually in lost revenue, with repairs expected to take approximately three years.
Developing alternative export infrastructure would require tens of billions of dollars in investment in pipelines and liquefaction facilities. Even such an expansion would not necessarily eliminate security risks, since additional energy infrastructure could itself become a target during future conflicts.
Qatar’s decision to secure overseas supplies therefore offers a different approach. Instead of relying exclusively on building more infrastructure at home, the country is diversifying the geography of its energy production and supply.
Qatar and the United States face a growing LNG rivalry
The timing of Qatar’s agreements is particularly significant because the country is preparing for its largest expansion of LNG production in decades.
The International Energy Agency estimates that approximately 300 billion cubic metres of new LNG export capacity will become available globally between 2025 and 2030, increasing total supply capacity by around 50%.
The United States is expected to account for more than half of this expansion, while Qatar is projected to contribute roughly another quarter.
This will place the two countries at the centre of the next phase of global LNG trade, intensifying competition for international customers and market share.
Qatar retains an important competitive advantage in production costs. Industry estimates put its LNG production costs at approximately $3 to $5 per million British thermal units, around half the cost of many US projects.
However, the United States has a different advantage: its LNG exports are not dependent on the Strait of Hormuz. For buyers increasingly concerned about geopolitical disruption, that distinction is becoming more important.
Energy markets have traditionally placed considerable emphasis on price and production costs. The Iran war has demonstrated that the security of supply can be just as important when countries make long-term purchasing decisions.
Consequently, US LNG may become more attractive to buyers seeking to reduce exposure to geopolitical risks, even when alternative suppliers offer lower production costs.
Can Qatar protect its LNG expansion from regional instability?
Qatar’s international purchasing strategy comes as it prepares to nearly double its LNG production capacity by 2030. The first new production trains are expected to begin operating early next year.
The central challenge is no longer simply whether Qatar can achieve its expansion targets. It is whether the country can maintain reliable operations and deliver its growing LNG volumes in an increasingly unstable regional environment.
Even if Washington and Tehran eventually reach a sustainable agreement, the Iran war may have permanently changed how energy markets assess the Strait of Hormuz. The assumption that the waterway will always provide reliable access to international markets has become much harder to maintain.
For Qatar, this creates a difficult strategic position. It remains one of the world’s most cost-competitive LNG producers and is preparing to expand its production substantially. Yet its dependence on a single export route exposes it to risks that additional domestic production alone cannot resolve.
Purchasing US LNG provides a way to maintain access to international supply networks while reducing dependence on facilities and shipping routes exposed to Gulf instability. It also gives Qatar an opportunity to benefit from growing demand for energy supplies perceived as more secure.
The wider implications extend beyond Qatar’s commercial strategy. The Iran conflict has accelerated a shift in global energy calculations, strengthening the position of the United States as a major LNG supplier while forcing Gulf producers to reconsider their exposure to regional security threats.
Qatar’s decision to buy gas from its growing competitor is therefore more than a commercial arrangement. It reflects an emerging energy order in which geographic diversification and security of supply are becoming as important as production capacity and price.
With information from Reuters.

articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Tuesday he reached a deal with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to end $4 billion in U.S. funding to Israel by the end of 2026. Speaking to Fox News' F...
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday he reached a deal with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to end $4 billion in U.S. funding to Israel by the end of 2026.
Speaking to Fox News' Fox and Friends, Trump said Israel no longer needed the funding and that some Democrats and left-wing politicians were using the U.S. financial support to Israel as a talking point to criticize Republicans.
"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump said.
"We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it," he added.
There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on Trump's remarks.
It was not immediately clear which exact funding Trump meant. A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion annual US military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028 and conversations have been under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
"They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," Trump said Tuesday.
Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off U.S. military support within a decade. In a June letter to a U.S. congressman he wrote that the time had come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."
U.S. public support for Israel has fallen since the genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of U.S. support for Israel.
"The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, well it's no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can't allow that to happen," Trump said.
"We were giving them 4 billion, we are, but it gets cut off at the end of the year," he said. "Why? Because they don't need it."

articles.title: Israel election body finds no vote fraud in blow to Netanyahu claims
articles.summary: Israel’s election commission revealed Wednesday it found no fraud in last week’s vote, undermining Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s attempts to discredit the results. Netanyahu...
articles.full_text:
Israel’s election commission revealed Wednesday it found no fraud in last week’s vote, undermining Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s attempts to discredit the results.
Netanyahu and his supporters have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
The results showed Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc losing its parliamentary majority, while Arab-led parties made substantial gains.
"The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results," the committee said in a statement.
The acting director of the elections committee, Dean Livne, said its investigation examined every complaint "individually and thoroughly," but found no evidence to support allegations that the election results were invalid.
The results, which are set to be formally certified Wednesday, "accurately reflect the choices voters made at the ballot box," Livne added.
A separate investigation by the Shin Bet intelligence service into allegations of foreign interference in the election is ongoing, according to a spokesperson for the elections committee.
The elections committee has said that while allegations that foreign actors may have sought to influence the election are serious, it does not believe any such interference affected the results of the election.
"Our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole," the head of the committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said Sunday.
Netanyahu’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
After receiving the certified results, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog will begin to meet Wednesday with each of the parties elected to parliament.
Following two days of consultations, he will choose the candidate – most likely Netanyahu or his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot – who he believes is best positioned to form a coalition government, setting the stage for weeks of negotiations.
Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's bloc of allies secured a parliamentary majority needed to form a new government. That raises the possibility of an alliance between the two rivals or an alliance between Eisenkot and some of the Arab-led parties. If neither man can put together a government, the country would hold a new election early next year.

articles.title: Israeli ex-generals stand with Palestinians amid settler violence
articles.summary: Former senior Israeli military officials joined Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday to help harvest olives, in a rare show of solidarity as escalating attacks...
articles.full_text:
Former senior Israeli military officials joined Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday to help harvest olives, in a rare show of solidarity as escalating attacks by illegal Israeli settler terrorists threaten Palestinian communities.
"When I see what is going on here, when I see these guys come... and hit women and kids, it reminds me of stories from my parents from the time when the Jewish people suffered," said former Major General Eyal Ben-Reuven, who compared the terrorist settler attacks to pogroms.
Ben-Reuven said he began organizing a group of around 30 senior military officials - including six generals - several months ago following an increase in settler violence that many Palestinians say is enabled by the Israeli military.
"Occupation is the main problem of Israeli society. I believe we must deal with it, we cannot ignore it. We must try to solve it together with the Palestinians," said former Colonel Doron Meinert.
Ben-Reuven and others said they were also concerned about the impact of settler violence on Israel's global reputation.
"Strategically, tactically, it's creating problems for the state of Israel in the West and the United States," said Jonatan Yoni, a former brigadier general, who said he was also motivated by the plight of Palestinian farmers and by opposition to Israeli annexation of the West Bank.
Nimr Nazzal, the owner of land near the village of Qusra where the ex-military personnel were helping out, said that without them it would be impossible for him to access his olives due to settler attacks.
He added that many of the settler attacks had the support of the Israeli military. "The army is protecting the settlers," said Nazzal.
The Israeli rights group Yesh Din has reported 180 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters over the 35 days since the season began. The Israeli military was present in more than 23% of the cases of settler violence it recorded, Yesh Din said.
Palestinians say that when they call the Israeli military, it either responds late or comes to the aid of the settlers perpetrating the violence.
Meinert, who now dedicates much of his time to volunteering in the West Bank in support of Palestinians, also said that the Israeli army aided the settlers.
Some Israeli soldiers, Meinert added, share the militant settlers' belief that only Jews "have the right to this area and that the Arabs should be expelled or stay here as second (class) residents".
The Israeli military has said in the past it is the people's army and reflects the full spectrum of views in Israeli society.
The West Bank is home to some 500,000 illegal Israeli settlers and at least 3 million Palestinians. U.N. bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law regarding military occupations.

- Digital Economy 2.0 report highlights Dubai’s platform for developing and scaling new financial technologies and forecasts a global FinTech market worth USD 1.5trn by 2030
Dubai, UAE: The inaugural Dubai Future Finance Week, led by Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), the leading global financial centre in the Middle East, Africa and South Asia (MEASA) region, continued today. The Dubai FinTech Summit has highlighted DIFC’s progress on innovation and new research focused on the future of finance, whilst other events in the programme moved decisively into climate transition finance, long-term capital deployment and alternative investment strategies.
Held under the directives and patronage of His Highness Sheikh Maktoum bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, First Deputy Ruler of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance of the UAE, and President of DIFC, Dubai Future Finance Week will advance the ambitions of the Dubai Economic Agenda D33, which aims to position Dubai among the top four global financial centres.
On day two of the Dubai FinTech Summit, His Excellency Arif Amiri, Chief Executive Officer of DIFC Authority, welcomed delegates and announced that, by offering the region’s most comprehensive proposition for AI, FinTech and innovation firms, DIFC is now home to more than 2,000 AI, FinTech and innovation companies.
The milestone comes less than ten years after DIFC launched its vision to drive the future of finance, anchored by the establishment of FinTech Hive, the region's first and largest financial technology accelerator.
His Excellency Arif Amiri, Chief Executive Officer of DIFC Authority, said: "FinTech has played a defining role in transforming financial services and remains central to the future of finance. DIFC’s thriving ecosystem now includes more than 2,000 AI, FinTech and innovation firms, reflecting Dubai’s determination to remain at the forefront of the industry. Our ambition is not simply to attract promising businesses, but to give them the environment, connections and capabilities they need to scale globally. We are now creating the conditions for the next wave of growth which will ensure we continue to position Dubai as the world’s number one city for FinTech.”
Reflecting DIFC’s long-term partnership with Julius Baer Group, the day’s signature session featured Noel Quinn, Chairman of the Board of Directors. Julius Baer was the first financial services firm to establish itself in the Centre in 2004.
Amongst the broad range of speakers on day two were: H.E. Dr. Tariq Bin Hendi, CEO and Board Member, Astra Tech; H.E. Dr. Fatih Karahan, Governor, Central Bank of Turkey; Hamed Ali, Chief Executive Officer, Dubai Financial Market and Nasdaq Dubai; H.E. Fahad Al Gergawi, Undersecretary of the Ministry of Foreign Trade, United Arab Emirates; and Toon Gyssels, CEO, Talabat.
Future of Finance: Digital Economy 2.0
During the Dubai FinTech Summit and reinforcing DIFC’s role in driving the future of finance, the Centre and its research partner Asia House launched the Digital Economy 2.0 report. Presented by Michael Lawrence OBE, Chief Executive Officer of Asia House, the report highlights the critical role of capital, talent, and progressive regulation in enabling the next phase of digital economic growth. It also underscores how Dubai's digitally enabled and innovation-focused environment provides a strong platform for the development and scaling of new financial technologies.
The report forecasts that global technology spending will reach USD 5.6trn in 2026, with artificial intelligence expected to contribute USD 22.3trn to the global economy by 2030. It also projects that the global FinTech market will grow to USD 1.5trn by 2030, highlighting the scale of opportunities emerging across digital finance, AI-driven services, and next-generation financial infrastructure.
Global financial leaders and institutional allocators are invited to engage with the remaining programme of Dubai Future Finance Week, which continues through Friday 6 November 2026. Upcoming forums and executive dialogues will focus on banking excellence, Islamic finance, family wealth, tokenisation, and digital assets. Nov 05: Dubai is expanding its ambitions in the global technology sector with the launch of Nad Zabeel, a new research, development and innovation (RDI) campus planned in Zabeel Park. The initiative reflects the emirate’s growing focus on attracting international technology companies, encouraging scientific research and creating opportunities for businesses working on future technologies.
Announced on November 1, 2026, Nad Zabeel is designed to bring researchers, universities, technology companies, investors and government organisations together in one environment. The campus will feature laboratories, scientific research centres and innovation incubators, providing infrastructure for developing and testing new ideas.
With artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, advanced technology, urban solutions, healthcare and environmental technologies among its focus areas, Dubai’s new R&D campus could become an important addition to the region’s innovation landscape.
For international businesses, the development also raises an interesting possibility: Dubai could become not just a destination for technology companies looking to expand, but also a place where they can invest in developing the technologies of tomorrow.
Nad Zabeel: A New Centre for Research and Innovation in Dubai
Nad Zabeel is planned as a collaborative research destination that connects scientific expertise with commercial opportunities. Instead of having researchers, universities and private companies operate independently, the campus aims to create an environment where they can work together on emerging technologies.
Located in Zabeel Park, the development will bring together laboratories, research facilities and creative innovation spaces. It is expected to host global technology companies, academic institutions, universities, investors and government organisations.
The project is being developed under the supervision of Dubai Future Foundation, with construction and associated operations expected to be completed within five years.
More than 30,000 scientists, researchers and entrepreneurs are expected to participate in its programmes and events annually. This could give international specialists more opportunities to connect with local businesses and explore research partnerships in the UAE.
The initiative is part of Dubai’s wider Research, Development and Innovation ecosystem, which aims to connect scientific research with economic and social priorities.
Why Dubai’s New R&D Campus Could Attract International Investors
For global technology companies, choosing a location for research and development involves more than infrastructure and office space. Access to skilled professionals, research facilities, funding networks and business partnerships can influence where companies establish their innovation operations.
Dubai is working to strengthen these advantages through investments in specialised technology infrastructure and initiatives designed to attract international businesses.
Nad Zabeel supports the objectives of the Dubai Economic Agenda D33, which aims to double the size of Dubai’s economy by 2033. Developing a stronger knowledge economy and attracting specialised investment are important parts of this ambition.
The new campus could create opportunities for international companies interested in establishing research partnerships, testing new products and exploring technology markets across the Middle East.
It could also make Dubai more attractive to businesses that want closer connections between research, investment and commercial development.
For investors, the opportunity extends to emerging technology businesses that may need financial support, technical expertise and industry partnerships to take their products to market.
Five Technology Sectors That Could Benefit From Nad Zabeel
Dubai’s new research infrastructure is expected to focus on several industries where technological development could create significant business opportunities.
1. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
AI is changing how businesses operate, from financial services and healthcare to logistics and manufacturing. Research partnerships could support the development of specialised AI applications, machine learning systems and intelligent automation tools.
Companies working on enterprise AI, data analytics and advanced computing may find opportunities to collaborate with researchers and technology developers in Dubai.
2. Robotics and Advanced Automation
Demand for robotics is growing across manufacturing, warehousing, logistics and infrastructure management. Research into autonomous systems and intelligent machines could encourage new partnerships between technology developers and businesses looking to improve operational efficiency.
This could create opportunities for companies specialising in industrial robotics, automation software and smart equipment.
3. Healthcare and Medical Technology
Healthcare innovation is another area with considerable potential. Digital diagnostics, medical devices, AI-assisted research and connected healthcare systems are attracting interest from technology businesses worldwide.
By bringing researchers and technology companies together, Nad Zabeel could support the development of solutions addressing healthcare challenges and improving service delivery.
4. Smart City and Urban Technologies
Dubai’s investment in modern infrastructure creates opportunities for businesses developing smart mobility systems, connected buildings, digital infrastructure and intelligent energy management.
Research collaborations could help companies test technologies that improve how cities manage transportation, public services and urban resources.
5. Environmental and Sustainability Technologies
Businesses working on clean technology, environmental monitoring, energy efficiency and resource management could also benefit from the development.
As governments and companies place greater emphasis on sustainable operations, research partnerships may help accelerate the development of practical solutions for industries and urban environments.
Business Opportunities for Startups and Global Technology Companies
One of the most important aspects of Nad Zabeel is its potential to connect businesses at different stages of development.
Startups often face difficulties accessing specialised research facilities, experienced professionals and potential investors. A dedicated innovation environment could help address some of these challenges by creating opportunities for collaboration and participation in incubator programmes.
For international technology companies, the campus could offer a platform to explore partnerships with UAE-based businesses, universities and government organisations.
Investors may also find opportunities to connect with emerging businesses working on AI, robotics, healthcare and sustainability solutions.
The location could be particularly relevant for companies looking to expand into the Middle East while maintaining connections with international research and investment networks.
However, specific partnership, funding and participation opportunities will depend on the programmes and arrangements announced as the project develops.
Dubai’s Existing Technology Ecosystem Strengthens the Opportunity
Nad Zabeel is entering an environment where Dubai has already made considerable investments in technology businesses and innovation.
The Dubai AI Campus, located within the Dubai International Financial Centre, provides an example of how specialised infrastructure can attract technology companies and investment.
Since its launch in May 2024, the campus has attracted more than 500 AI companies. These businesses have collectively secured over AED 1 billion in investment and contributed to the creation of more than 2,000 specialised technology jobs.
In October 2026, Dubai approved new targets for the AI Campus to attract more than 1,000 companies and create over 5,000 specialised jobs by 2030.
Other established business destinations, including Dubai Internet City and Dubai International Financial Centre, provide access to technology businesses, financial institutions and international investors.
Nad Zabeel could complement these developments by adding a stronger research and scientific development dimension to the existing ecosystem.
This combination of business infrastructure, research facilities and investment networks could help Dubai attract companies looking beyond conventional regional office operations.
Challenges That Could Influence the Project’s Success
While the proposed campus offers considerable potential, attracting long-term research investment will require more than modern laboratories and specialised facilities.
Access to experienced researchers and engineers will be important. Dubai will also need strong relationships with international universities, scientific institutions and private-sector organisations.
Funding opportunities, intellectual property protection and clear regulatory processes will influence how attractive the environment becomes for businesses developing new technologies.
Another important factor will be the ability to turn research into commercially successful products. Companies will want to see practical outcomes, opportunities for collaboration and a clear path from product development to market adoption.
