articles.title: Trump admits Iran war fueled Republican midterm election losses
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged that the war with Iran was a major factor behind Republicans' crushing midterm election losses, echoing Vice President JD Vanc...
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged that the war with Iran was a major factor behind Republicans' crushing midterm election losses, echoing Vice President JD Vance's call for the party to confront the political fallout from the increasingly unpopular conflict.
Asked if he agreed with Vance's remark that the Iran war was "the reason we lost," Trump, speaking to reporters at his White House ballroom construction site, said: "I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term."
"But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again. Because long term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he added.
The midterm election blowout delivered a new era in Washington, with Democrats in Congress eager to meet voter demands for change while Republicans watched their majorities evaporate after a revolt against President Donald Trump and his party in power.
Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast, with many surprising places in between, in a decisive rejection of unified GOP control for the promise of something different for the country. Their majorities will be padded by unusually wide margins in both the House and the Senate.
The staggering results are setting up a starkly divided government, with an emboldened Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch when Democrats take over in the new year. They are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower the costs of gas, groceries and healthcare and conduct vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration, with impeachment an option.

articles.title: Trump lost both war and political battle after US midterms: Iran
articles.summary: Iran's top security official Mohsen Rezai on Wednesday declared that U.S. President Donald Trump had suffered defeats both on the battlefield against Tehran and at home, pointing t...
articles.full_text:
Iran's top security official Mohsen Rezai on Wednesday declared that U.S. President Donald Trump had suffered defeats both on the battlefield against Tehran and at home, pointing to Republican losses in the midterm elections as evidence of a broader political setback.
"The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz – and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington," Rezai, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said on X.
Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei claimed that Tehran had inflicted military and political defeats on US President Donald Trump.
"The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz-and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington," Rezaei wrote on X.
He also said Americans were bearing the financial burden of the war.
"Anyone who takes on Iran will pay the price-from the battlefield to their own doorstep," he warned.
The remarks came after U.S. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war with Iran for Republicans' defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote on X on Wednesday, saying voter anger over the conflict had driven former Trump supporters to back Democrats.
Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress in the elections.
The U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, before a ceasefire was reached in April. Fighting resumed in July amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.

articles.title: US VP Vance blames Iran war for Republican midterm election losses
articles.summary: U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday blamed Republican losses in the midterm elections on growing public frustration over the war with Iran, saying opposition to the conflict...
articles.full_text:
U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday blamed Republican losses in the midterm elections on growing public frustration over the war with Iran, saying opposition to the conflict had pushed voters who previously supported President Donald Trump toward Democrats.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote in a statement on X.
He argued that the election results reflected dissatisfaction with the administration's foreign policy rather than low Republican voter turnout.
Vance said many Americans who supported President Donald Trump and himself in the 2024 presidential election switched to the Democratic Party in 2026, despite significant turnout among Republican voters.
"The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026," he said.
Citing polling data, Vance said voters who abandoned Republicans identified ending the war, tackling the cost of living and inflation, putting America first and changing Washington's relationship with Israel as their main concerns.
The vice president acknowledged that Republicans would face "a lot of infighting and arguing" over the reasons behind their electoral losses.
He also conceded that the party's economic messaging may have fallen short but maintained that the Iran war was the central factor behind the defeat.
"Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance said.
The Democratic wave in Tuesday's midterms has raised major questions over Vance's previous status as the frontrunner for the Republican nomination in the 2028 presidential election.
He has not yet formally declared that he will run.
Vance, a longtime vocal critic of U.S. foreign interventionism, had reportedly been skeptical behind the scenes about the war on Iran that Trump and Israel launched in late February.
In the weeks ahead, the parties will hold internal leadership elections as members-elect arrive for freshman orientation at the Capitol.
The House will choose its speaker as one of the first votes when the new Congress convenes.
Rarely has the president's party held on to power during midterm elections, but the Democratic sweep carried echoes of Trump's first term, when Republicans faced a voter revolt that sent Democrats to the House majority, and the Barack Obama era, when the Republican tea party swept to power.
This new Congress will also mark firsts and welcome trailblazers.

articles.title: Iran’s Khamenei sees no shift in US policy after Democratic wins
articles.summary: Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, said Wednesday that anyone expecting U.S. policy toward Iran to change after Democrats won control of Congress was “seriously mis...
articles.full_text:
Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, said Wednesday that anyone expecting U.S. policy toward Iran to change after Democrats won control of Congress was “seriously mistaken,” even as Tehran’s chief negotiator welcomed the midterm results as a vote against the war.
"Those who still harbor even the slightest hope that the behavior of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility toward the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken," Khamenei said in a written statement published on his website.
Democrats won both the House and Senate in Tuesday's elections amid voter discontent over the cost of living, President Donald Trump's tariffs and a war that has driven up fuel prices.
The United States and Israel have threatened in recent days to resume attacks on Iran as diplomatic efforts continue to avert a return to full-scale fighting.
The war began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28 and has been at a stalemate for months, interrupted by sporadic exchanges of fire.
“Should such aggressions be repeated, the war's scope will become much wider," Khamenei said.
Earlier Wednesday, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the United States, said he saw opposition to the war in the election results.
"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Ghalibaf wrote on X.
"If the U.S. govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."
Iranian judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei also welcomed the outcome, saying Trump had been "defeated both militarily and politically."
"We will certainly inflict further defeats on him," he added.
Khamenei, 57, became supreme leader in March after U.S. and Israeli strikes killed his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, at the start of the war.
He has communicated through written messages and has yet to appear in public since taking office.

articles.title: Israeli opposition slams Netanyahu over Trump's decision to end US aid
articles.summary: Israeli opposition leaders accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of jeopardizing the country's security and economy Tuesday after U.S. President Donald Trump announced plans to...
articles.full_text:
Israeli opposition leaders accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of jeopardizing the country's security and economy Tuesday after U.S. President Donald Trump announced plans to end American financial assistance to Israel by the end of 2026, a move that reportedly caught senior Israeli defense and finance officials off guard.
Former military chief and opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot called for Netanyahu's removal, saying the government's failure to inform key institutions of the impending shift exposed serious flaws in its handling of relations with Washington.
"The fact that Israel's defence establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media, at the same time as the Israeli public, shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct is," Eisenkot said in a statement.
"He can no longer be trusted and must be replaced," he added.
Yair Golan, leader of Israel's Democrats party, also condemned the development, describing it as another major failure by Netanyahu at a time when Israel faces mounting military expenditures and pressure to replenish weapons stockpiles following prolonged regional conflicts.
In a statement posted on X, Golan warned that the loss of American assistance would place an additional financial burden on Israeli taxpayers while weakening the country's ability to meet its defense requirements.
"Israel's air defense capabilities have been depleted after such a prolonged war," he said, arguing that the government should have sought greater support from Washington rather than allowing existing assistance to end.
"A responsible prime minister would have fought to increase US assistance, not end it," Golan said.
He accused Netanyahu of aggravating Israel's economic and security challenges and putting the country's long-term stability at risk.
Trump announced earlier Tuesday that Washington would discontinue financial assistance to Israel by the end of the year, citing an agreement he said had been reached with Netanyahu several months earlier.
The announcement came as Americans voted in congressional midterm elections, with all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats at stake.
Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported that senior officials in the Defense Ministry and military were surprised by Trump's remarks, raising questions about whether the country's security establishment had been consulted about the decision.
Channel 12 reported separately that Finance Ministry officials were also unaware of the planned cutoff before the president's public announcement.
The reported lack of coordination fueled criticism from opposition politicians, who questioned the government's transparency and preparedness for a significant change in Israel's relationship with its principal military backer.
Under a 2016 memorandum of understanding, Washington pledged $38 billion in military assistance to Israel over 10 years through 2028, equivalent to approximately $3.8 billion annually.
The funding had been expected to remain a major component of Israel's defense financing in 2027 and 2028, according to Channel 12.
Netanyahu has previously advocated reducing Israel's reliance on American military assistance and expanding domestic weapons production, arguing that greater self-sufficiency would strengthen the country's strategic independence.
However, opposition leaders warned that an abrupt withdrawal of U.S. support could intensify budgetary pressures at a time of elevated defense spending.
The dispute comes amid political uncertainty following Israel's parliamentary elections.
According to the reported results, Netanyahu's bloc secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for opposition parties and 19 for Arab parties.
Neither major bloc holds the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority, potentially leaving Arab lawmakers with a decisive role in coalition negotiations.
Israel's Central Elections Committee is expected to announce the official final results Wednesday.
The controversy over U.S. assistance adds another challenge for Netanyahu as opposition figures seek to capitalize on growing concerns over his government's management of national security, public finances and relations with Washington.

articles.title: Israeli oppositions discuss ousting Netanyahu in nod for Eisenkot
articles.summary: Leaders of the Arab Joint List and Israel’s Democrats party agreed Tuesday to coordinate efforts to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government after their first meeting...
articles.full_text:
Leaders of the Arab Joint List and Israel’s Democrats party agreed Tuesday to coordinate efforts to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government after their first meeting since last week’s Knesset elections.
Joint List Chairman Yousef Jabareen and parliamentary group leader Ahmad Tibi met Democrats leader Yair Golan to assess the political situation following the Oct. 27 election results and discuss coordination between their blocs, the Arab Joint List said in a statement.
According to preliminary results, Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while opposition parties secured 48 seats. Arab parties won 19 seats, with the Joint List securing 11 and Ra’am obtaining eight.
The two sides stressed their "shared interest in using the parliamentary majority to bring down the Netanyahu-Ben-Gvir-Smotrich government and replace it," according to the statement.
Jabareen and Tibi also raised key issues facing Arab citizens of Israel and discussed steps aimed at advancing "practical and tangible solutions," the statement said.
Arabs make up around 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
The two sides agreed to continue communication and coordination ahead of upcoming political steps, strengthen parliamentary cooperation and advance what the statement described as an agenda based on "equality and peace."
Israeli President Isaac Herzog is scheduled to hold consultations Wednesday and Thursday with parties represented in the Knesset before deciding which lawmaker to task with forming the next government.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, who heads the opposition Change bloc, could receive the largest number of recommendations if he secures the support of Arab lawmakers.
Golan is one of the leaders of the Change bloc.
Netanyahu, 76, has served five nonconsecutive terms as prime minister, making him Israel’s longest-serving premier.
He has led the current government since late 2022, heading a coalition widely described as the most far-right in Israel’s history.
Netanyahu is currently on trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which could carry prison sentences if he is convicted.
He is also wanted by the International Criminal Court under an arrest warrant issued in 2024 over accusations of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Israel's genocidal war there since October 2023 have killed more than 74,500 Palestinians, mostly women and children.

articles.title: US 'defensive' strikes hit Iranian island despite diplomatic push
articles.summary: Just hours after President Donald Trump signaled diplomatic progress with Tehran, the U.S. launched Tuesday what it called "defensive" strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of...
articles.full_text:
Just hours after President Donald Trump signaled diplomatic progress with Tehran, the U.S. launched Tuesday what it called "defensive" strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. media reported.
The strikes, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, hit Qeshm Island, where Iranian state media reported five explosions in rapid succession.
U.S. officials, cited by the Journal and other outlets, described the attacks as defensive. The Journal said the strikes were the latest of several undeclared and had not been publicly announced to avoid the impression Washington intended to resume major combat operations. U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to an Agence France-Presse (AFP) request for comment.
The U.S. and Israel launched the war with surprise strikes on Iran in late February, but have not achieved their war aims and the conflict has stalled for months.
On Monday, a day before voters were expected to hand his Republican party a drubbing in midterm elections in part over dissatisfaction with the war and the inflation it has brought, President Donald Trump said a deal with Iran "could happen."
"Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible," Trump posted on his Truth Social.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said indirect talks were underway.
"Given the sensitivity and gravity of the current situation, consultations and deliberations are intensive," Araghchi told state media.
On Tuesday, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Tehran's chief negotiator in talks with the U.S., said while Iran was ready for war it had given Washington a "rational response."
"The ball is now in America's court to prevent war."
Oil prices plunged more than 7% Monday on optimism over a possible end to the eight-month conflict.
U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance said both he and Trump were optimistic about securing an agreement.
"We've certainly made some progress. We'll see if we can make some more," Vance told reporters Monday.
China also called for a return to diplomacy, while Iran's security chief discussed the conflict with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Last week, Axios reported that Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks, marking the highest-level move in months.
Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said messages from Washington were "an acknowledgement of our victory."
A senior Iranian official said Tehran was ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and gas supplies, within two days but only if Washington agreed to its long-standing list of demands.
In September, Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen the strait, with demands including ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
"The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran's good-faith approach," Tehran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters at a briefing.
China held meetings with Iranian and Saudi officials in Beijing Monday.
Beijing supports Tehran in "safeguarding its own sovereignty and security," Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Ali Bagheri, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, according to a Chinese statement.
In an interview with Al Jazeera released Sunday, Foreign Minister Araghchi said Washington must accept a new route agreed by Iran and Oman for transiting the strait.
He said Washington must also remove recently imposed sanctions and reduce U.S. troop numbers in the region.
Trump has kept up his threats against Tehran, saying Sunday the United States may have to give Iran "the hammer" at some unspecified time.
On Saturday, the U.S. leader said he still had to "take care" of one or two targets including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.
Iranian officials have repeatedly warned of wide-ranging retaliation if the U.S. resumes the war.
Authorities in Tehran installed a large banner in the heart of the capital, AFP journalists said Tuesday.
Over a photo of the U.S. president, it reads: "We will kill Trump."

Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of Iranian parliament’s security committee, said Iran would fire on any European base used against it, including in Italy and Germany. State-run media said any new confrontation could reach “the heart of Europe".
Iranian lawmakers have threatened missile strikes on European countries hosting US military bases, as state-run media warned on Wednesday that any renewed confrontation with the US could reach "the heart of Europe".
"If America uses its bases in Europe, including in Italy and Germany, Iran's missiles will be fired towards Europe," Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of parliament's National Security Committee, told Euronews.
"In the two previous wars we did not do this, but this time we will not let Europe's assistance to America for an attack on Iran go without consequence;" Ardestani added.
Asked whether Europe was entering a new phase of war with Iran, Ardestani said European countries had already been at war with Iran in the previous phase by allowing their bases to be used.
He said Iran would strike any base used against it and would also target "the material and non-material assets of countries that assist America."
A second committee member, Fada Hossein Maleki, said Iran had prepared a new approach and scenario for any renewed conflict that he believed would surprise both the US and European countries.
German embassy message
The IRGC issued a statement on Wednesday — the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the US embassy in Tehran, marked in Iran as "the day of fighting global arrogance" — pledging "an immediate, effective response without geographical limits to every level and type of threat."
The statement cited orders attributed to Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei calling for updating Iran's "target bank" and placing "the enemy's material and non-material assets within range."
Ahead of Wednesday's anniversary marches, government supporters hung a banner outside the German embassy in Tehran carrying a quote from the secretary of Iran's National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, "Europe will pay the price for supporting Israel."
IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency identified those responsible as members of the student Basij at the University of Tehran.
Euronews sought comment from the German embassy in Tehran and Germany's foreign ministry on whether the banner had been placed on the embassy railings. Both were unreachable at the time of publication.
Fars reported separately that Iran had warned Germany its military assets across the region would be treated as "legitimate defensive targets" if Berlin entered open military confrontation with Iran. The claim could not be independently verified.
Tehran has summoned Germany's ambassador in recent weeks over Berlin's support for Israel.
Kayhan newspaper, published under the supervision of a representative of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, wrote that Iran's range of potential targets was no longer confined to US bases in the Middle East and could extend to "the heart of Europe," citing an order attributed to Khamenei for a "military response without geographical limits."
Rezaei wrote on X that the US response to Iran's demands had been "not convincing," saying Washington would need to meet Iran's seven conditions in full before reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf welcomed the Republicans' defeat in Tuesday's congressional elections in a post on X, writing that the American people had "said no to war" and that Iran supported that message.
"If the US government ignores the public will in order to act in favour of managers who pay bribes and engage in international blackmail, it will realise that our 'no' comes with a nightmare," Ghalibaf added.
Asked whether he planned to take a tougher line against Iran, US President Donald Trump gave an ambiguous answer, saying he would examine the matter and act if needed.

articles.title: For U.S. Iran Policy to Succeed, It Must Look Beyond Tehran - THE INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS REVIEW
articles.summary: For U.S. Iran Policy to Succeed, It Must Look Beyond Tehran  THE INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS REVIEW
articles.full_text:
Introduction: What Really Defines a U.S. Victory in Iran?
According to a Pew Research Center survey conducted from September 28 to October 4, 2026, 65 percent of Americans disapprove of President Donald Trump’s handling of the Iran War, with 47 percent anticipating that the war will last for more than another year.
The question is: What amounts to a U.S. victory in Iran?
U.S. Vice President JD Vance stated that the administration’s current priority is to curb Iranian uranium enrichment, which could potentially be used to develop nuclear weapons. However, Iran-backed proxy groups could prevent the United States from simply stepping away from the conflict.
U.S. Objectives and the Threat of Iran-Backed Proxies
On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran through Operation Epic Fury, a joint operation targeting Iranian officials, military capabilities, missile infrastructure, and key nuclear sites.
Despite the February strikes and subsequent military operations, nuclear nonproliferation remains a U.S. concern due to Iran’s history of concealing nuclear activities, disputes over its international nuclear obligations, and its continued development of long-range ballistic missiles. These concerns extend to regional partners, including Israel, Jordan, and the Gulf states, due to their geographic vulnerability to potential Iranian attacks.
In the early 1980s, during the Lebanese Civil War, Iran supported the emergence of Hezbollah, a militant organization developed to counter Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon at the time, establishing its first major proxy in the region. Since then, Iran has developed relationships with other anti-U.S. and anti-Israel groups, including Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), the Houthis, and militias in Iraq.
Iran provides funding, training, and military equipment to extend its influence beyond its borders. These groups have different missions, with Hezbollah and Hamas targeting Israel, the Houthis targeting the Gulf states, and Iraqi militias targeting U.S. forces. Many groups have also established significant political influence.
Despite Iran’s potential weakening, these groups may retain political power and pursue independent ambitions, complicating U.S. and regional efforts to achieve lasting security.
Lessons from Iraq in 2003 and the U.S.’s Dilemma
In 2003, President George W. Bush believed Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, prompting an invasion that overthrew Saddam Hussein and removed the Ba’ath Party from power. However, the suspected WMD stockpiles were never found, and the United States remained in Iraq until 2011.
The U.S. invasion and its de-Baathification policy contributed to sectarian conflict, insurgencies, and the development of al-Qaeda in Iraq (AQI), which eventually evolved into ISIS. Although President Barack Obama withdrew U.S. troops from Iraq in 2011, ISIS’s expansion prompted U.S. troops to return in 2014. Non-state actors continued to shape U.S. involvement even after its initial intervention in 2003.
The United States continues to balance its enforcement of nuclear nonproliferation objectives with regional security. Significantly reducing Iranian uranium enrichment may help end the war, but it would not eliminate threats posed by Iran-backed groups.
Given what happened in Iraq and the persistence of Iran-backed proxies, two questions remain even if the United States achieves its nonproliferation goals in Iran:
What stops Iran-backed proxies from continuing to weaken the United States and its regional allies through attacks on military forces, critical infrastructure, and economic interests? And why would reducing uranium enrichment be enough to secure a peace agreement that ends regional conflict and prevents renewed U.S. military intervention?
The Iraq War illustrates that achieving initial military goals does not prevent non-state actors from drawing the United States into prolonged regional conflict.
Historical and Contemporary Limitations of a Nuclear Deal
Halting Iranian uranium enrichment should remain a national security concern for the United States and its regional allies. A potential nuclear weapon in Iran’s hands would pose a significant threat to regional and international security. However, a nuclear agreement alone may not guarantee a lasting end to the current war or U.S. involvement.
Previous nuclear diplomatic efforts with Iran have failed to produce a lasting resolution, and disputes over compliance have repeatedly resurfaced. The two major international arrangements relevant to Iran’s nuclear program are the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1970 and the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) of 2015.
Under the NPT, non-nuclear-weapon states committed to neither producing nuclear weapons nor assisting another state in their production. Iran has been a party to the treaty since 1970; however, after the Iranian Revolution in 1979 and the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s, Tehran resumed its nuclear program partly in response to perceived Iraqi weapons threats. In 2025, Iran’s parliament adopted legislation to suspend cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), further raising concerns over Iranian compliance with its nuclear obligations.
The JCPOA illustrates the challenges of sustaining nuclear restrictions. The agreement required Iran to dismantle parts of its nuclear infrastructure and accept IAEA verification in exchange for sanctions relief. Iran complied initially; however, after the United States exited the agreement in 2018 over concerns around Iran’s ballistic missile program and regional proxies, Iran began expanding its enrichment activities in 2019, primarily at Fordow and subsequently at Natanz.
While nuclear agreements are important for preventing Iranian nuclear proliferation, their limitations demonstrate why the United States must address regional security separately. Nuclear weapons remain a valid concern when considering Iran’s capabilities, but an agreement will not eliminate U.S. security commitments to Israel, Jordan, and Gulf partners or the threats posed by Iran-backed proxy groups.
Path to Sustainable Victory in the Region: Looking Past Tehran
The United States should pursue three strategies to reduce the likelihood of prolonged military involvement in the region:
1) Strengthen allied military capabilities through training and intelligence systems.
As a first line of defense, the United States should expand joint military exercises with regional allies, including Israel, Jordan, and the Gulf states, to improve deterrence and defensive coordination while bolstering their command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (C4ISR) capabilities. This strategy should prioritize early-warning systems and missile and drone defenses against attacks by Iran-backed groups.
2) Develop a greater regional defense strategy.
The United States should expand existing security and intelligence cooperation agreements to incorporate greater intelligence sharing, joint threat assessments, and coordinated responses. Regular communication between military and intelligence officials could strengthen regional security while reducing the need for U.S. intervention.
3) Increase diplomatic dialogue.
The United States should pursue diplomatic discussions with Tehran and regional partners through separate or mediated negotiations when direct talks are unrealistic. Where feasible and considered absolutely necessary, diplomatic engagement should also extend to Iran-backed proxy groups, recognizing their political influence and independent interests. Negotiations should address Iranian nuclear activities, proxy violence, and respect for state sovereignty. Military force should remain a last resort.
_____________________________________________________________________________
Even with these three strategies, future U.S. military involvement may remain necessary. However, through intentional preparation, regional cooperation, and diplomacy, the United States may be able to reduce the likelihood of prolonged intervention. A sustainable victory must look beyond Tehran.
Staff Editor: Carly Gordon
Managing Editor: Emma Hopp

Dubai, UAE: Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), the leading global financial centre in the Middle East, Africa and South Asia (MEASA) region, has entered into a strategic partnership with Mizuho Financial Group to accelerate innovation, strengthen UAE-Japan economic cooperation, and support the international expansion of Japanese start-ups and innovation-led businesses.
Witnessed by His Excellency Essa Kazim, Governor of DIFC, the agreement was signed by His Excellency Arif Amiri, Chief Executive Officer of DIFC Authority, and Suneel Bakhshi, Deputy Group CEO at Mizuho, in the presence of senior executives from both DIFC and Mizuho Financial Group.

articles.title: Top 5 Business Setup Consultants in UAE Trusted by Foreign Investors - StreetInsider

articles.full_text:
If you are planning to start a business in the UAE from abroad, you will quickly notice that the hard part is not the paperwork itself. It is knowing which route to take. Mainland or free zone? Which licence fits your activity? How many visas do you need, and how long will a bank account take? The answers shape your costs, your timeline and what your company can legally do.
That is why most foreign investors work with a business setup consultant or go directly to a free zone authority. Both routes work, but they do different jobs. Consultants advise across jurisdictions and handle the process for you, while free zone authorities issue the licence and provide the business environment.
Here are five names that come up often when international founders research their options, along with what each one is best suited for.
1. Avyanco: End-to-End Business Setup Support in the UAE
Avyanco is a Dubai-based business setup and corporate services consultancy, founded in 2020 and headquartered on Level 36 of Burj Al Salam Tower on Sheikh Zayed Road. It works with entrepreneurs, start-ups, SMEs and established groups entering the UAE, and supports clients across Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah, with access to more than 45 free zones, including DMCC, IFZA, JAFZA, DAFZA, DIFC, Meydan and ADGM.
For anyone planning a Company Setup in Dubai, the firm’s work starts with structure. Its advisers look at whether your business needs a mainland licence to trade with local customers, a free zone licence for international trade and services, or an offshore entity for holding purposes. That one decision affects everything that follows, from visa allocation to banking.
Once the structure is clear, Avyanco takes care of the steps that usually slow overseas founders down: trade name reservation, initial approvals, licence issuance, memorandum of association, investor and employee visas, medical tests, biometrics and Emirates ID. Its PRO team handles government liaison, document clearing and attestation, so much of the process can move forward before you relocate. Residency support also covers Golden Visa applications, dependent visas, renewals and cancellations.
Cost is usually the first question founders ask, and the firm deals with it upfront. Avyanco explains that the Company formation cost in Dubai varies with the jurisdiction, activity, number of visas and office requirement, and it provides itemised quotes and an online cost calculator so you can compare options before you commit.
The support continues after the licence is issued. Avyanco helps with corporate bank account applications, corporate tax registration at the 0% and 9% rates, VAT registration and filing, bookkeeping, payroll and WPS, CFO services and audit. For more complex needs, it advises on holding companies, SPVs, family foundations, transfer pricing, AML compliance and UBO filing.
Its reach goes beyond the UAE too. Avyanco supports company formation in markets including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, India, Singapore, Hong Kong, the UK and the US, which is useful if you are building a Gulf base alongside operations elsewhere. The firm holds a 4.8-star rating from more than 700 Google reviews, and you can read more about its process on its page covering business setup in Dubai.
2. JAFZA
Jebel Ali Free Zone, known as JAFZA, began operations in 1985 and is operated by DP World. Spread across about 57 square kilometres beside Jebel Ali Port, it hosts companies from more than 150 countries, ranging from regional distributors to global manufacturers. The free zone offers offices, warehouses, light industrial units and land plots, which makes it a practical base for businesses that move physical goods. Its location also gives companies direct access to Al Maktoum International Airport, around 24 kilometres away, so sea and air freight can be combined easily. It is important to note that JAFZA is a free zone authority rather than a consultancy, so investors apply to it directly or through a setup adviser.
3. Sovereign Group
Sovereign Group was established in 1987 and now operates across more than 20 jurisdictions worldwide. In the UAE, it holds corporate service provider licences in DIFC, DMCC, ADGM, RAK International Corporate Centre and the Dubai mainland, with a team working from offices in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Its company formation work covers mainland, free zone and offshore structures, including trading companies, holding SPVs and branch offices of foreign businesses. Alongside formation, the group supports residency through employment, investor and Golden Visas, as well as retirement and remote work visa options. Its private client team also works on trusts and foundations for asset protection and succession planning, which sets it apart from firms focused only on licensing.
4. Synergy Gulf
Synergy Gulf is a Dubai-based business consultancy that, according to business directory listings, has operated since 2013. Its core services include company formation and local partnership arrangements for activities that require them. The firm also offers business planning, helping founders shape a market-entry idea into a structured plan before they apply for a licence. Its corporate advisory work covers strategy, compliance and regulatory matters for companies operating in the Middle East. The firm describes its client base as ranging from small businesses to larger international companies.
5. Meydan Free Zone
Meydan Free Zone is located a few minutes from Downtown Dubai and has built its offer around a fully digital setup process. Applications, document uploads and licence issuance are handled online, so founders can register a company without visiting in person. The free zone lists more than 2,500 business activities and allows up to three activity groups to be combined on a single licence. Its Fawri option issues a licence within 60 minutes, while the regular route typically takes one to three business days. Companies can be set up as an FZE, an FZCO or a branch of a foreign company, and like JAFZA, Meydan is a licensing authority rather than a consultancy.
How to Choose the Right Business Setup Partner in the UAE
Start with what your business actually needs to do in the UAE. A trading company selling to local customers will usually need a mainland licence. A consultancy invoicing overseas clients may suit a free zone. A holding structure may need something else entirely. A consultant helps you compare these routes, while a free zone authority gives you the licence, the address and the ecosystem.
Next, look closely at the numbers. Headline package prices rarely include every government fee, visa cost or office charge, and second-year renewals can differ from the first. Ask for a written quote that lists every inclusion, exclusion and annual renewal figure.
Finally, check what happens after setup. Corporate tax registration, VAT thresholds and ongoing filings are now part of running a UAE company, so make sure your provider is properly licensed and can support you with banking, tax and compliance, not just the licence.
Final Thoughts on Choosing a UAE Business Setup Consultant
There is no single right choice for every investor. If you already know your jurisdiction, going directly to a free zone such as JAFZA or Meydan can work well. If you want guidance across licensing, visas, banking and tax, an advisory firm such as Avyanco, will save you time and avoid costly mistakes. Either way, the best decision comes from matching the structure to your business model, budget and long-term plans.

articles.title: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes  Al JazeeraIran plays down hope for deal to end war after new U.S. strikes on eve of midterm elections  CBS NewsTehran’s factions weigh Doha talks as hardliners prepare the public for war  Iran InternationalIran Says It Would Reopen Strait of Hormuz in 2 Days as Part of U.S. Deal  The New York TimesIran says contacts over ending war continue after talks finish with no breakthrough&nbs...
articles.full_text:
Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process“.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
Attack on Qeshm Island
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
Tanker struck in Hormuz
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while attempting to pass through a prohibited shipping lane south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The tankers remained ablaze following the explosions, the IRGC said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency. Two other vessels were detained for violating shipping restrictions, it added.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
It could not be independently verified whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and the IRGC were linked.
The IRGC also claimed its air defence forces shot down a US-made MQ-9 drone over the strait at 4.30am local time (01:00GMT), describing it as the 56th such aircraft it had downed.
The statement said the operations were carried out by the IRGC’s naval and aerospace forces, which had inflicted “heavy blows on the enemy”.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

articles.summary: ZAWYA: S&P affirms Qatar’s ‘AA/A-1+’ credit rating, maintains stable outlook  TradingView
articles.full_text:
By Staff Writer
Doha, Qatar: S&P Global Ratings has affirmed Qatar’s long- and short-term sovereign credit ratings at ‘AA/A-1+’, maintaining a stable outlook.
The ratings agency said Qatar’s substantial fiscal and external assets, strong financial buffers and flexibility in government spending would help the country withstand security and trade disruptions linked to the ongoing Middle East conflict.
S&P also maintained Qatar’s transfer and convertibility assessment at ‘AA+’, reflecting its assessment of the country’s ability to meet its financial obligations despite regional uncertainties.
The agency highlighted Qatar’s considerable financial reserves, particularly assets held through the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), as a major source of protection against external shocks.
S&P estimates the government’s liquid assets at approximately 200 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), including its assessment of QIA assets and government deposits in the banking system.
Additionally, Qatar Central Bank’s gross foreign exchange reserves stood at $60.6bn at the end of August 2026, while foreign currency liquidity amounted to approximately $11.5bn.
According to S&P, these financial resources provide the government with significant capacity to manage market volatility, support economic stability and finance recovery efforts during and after periods of regional disruption.
The agency stated that it expects the economy to begin recovering in 2027 as gas production moves closer to pre-conflict levels.
S&P also pointed to the resilience of Qatar’s non-hydrocarbon economy, which recorded growth of 3 percent during the first half of 2026. It expects this sector to remain resilient, supported partly by the economic benefits generated by the expansion of LNG production.
Government spending flexibility and relatively low public debt levels were also identified as important factors supporting Qatar’s creditworthiness.
Government expenditure reached QR95bn in the first half of 2026, representing a 14 percent decline compared with the corresponding period last year.
S&P noted that Qatar has previously demonstrated fiscal discipline during periods of economic pressure, reducing expenditure by 6 percent in 2014 and 15 percent in 2015 during an oil price downturn. Spending was also reduced by 8 percent during the 2017 and 12 percent during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The agency expects the government to maintain a prudent spending approach, helping contain the impact of potential revenue shortfalls. Combined with an anticipated recovery in LNG production, this is expected to support a return to fiscal surpluses from 2027.
A key driver of the projected recovery will be Qatar’s ambitious LNG expansion programme. The country plans to increase its annual LNG production capacity from the current 77 million tonnes to 142 million tonnes by 2030, representing an increase of almost 85 percent.
“We forecast Qatar’s economic growth will rebound from 2027, supported by the ongoing expansion of LNG production, from an estimated 14% contraction in 2026. We forecast real GDP growth will sharply recover to 15% in 2027, followed by an average growth rate of 8% over 2028-2029, as new gas production comes online, as per our base-case scenario. Despite ongoing disruptions in LNG production, we expect the North Field expansion to go ahead, albeit with some delays,” it noted.
The agency added that rising energy demand from rapidly developing Asian economies, together with LNG’s role as a transitional fuel in the global energy transition, would support Qatar’s export prospects.
Higher global oil and gas prices amid supply disruptions could also strengthen the country’s economic performance and improve its fiscal and external balances from 2027.
S&P’s assessment underscores the importance of Qatar’s accumulated financial reserves, energy sector strength and prudent fiscal management in supporting its sovereign credit profile amid an uncertain regional environment.

articles.title: How a new Israeli government could reshape the sountry's foreign policy - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: How a new Israeli government could reshape the sountry's foreign policy  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
As Israelis headed to the polls, domestic debate largely overlooked a key question: How much could new leadership change Israeli foreign policy? At first glance, very little.
Since October 7, 2023, Israelis have expected their government to confront threats before they reach the country’s doorstep. Those security priorities are unlikely to change soon; what may change is how Israel pursues them.
The current government has too often failed to turn military gains into durable political arrangements. A successor less dependent on the far-right could rebuild international trust and pair force more effectively with diplomacy.
Regarding Iran, the basic posture is unlikely to change.
A successor government would inherit deep distrust of Tehran and strong pressure to maintain a hard line. That would leave limited political room for negotiations, while the need to coordinate with Washington would continue to shape Israel’s military options. Israel is therefore likely to keep up pressure on Tehran, with close US coordination on military action.
Distrust also constrains policy toward the Palestinians. Many Israelis view the 2005 Gaza withdrawal and Hamas’s 2007 takeover as warnings about territorial concessions. Although Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas has condemned the October 7 attacks, distrust of the PA persists.
Washington says payments to convicted attackers and their families continue despite announced reforms. A successor would be unlikely to pursue a comprehensive peace agreement or major territorial concessions in the near term.
That need not preclude practical cooperation: security coordination with the PA continued during the war, even under Israel’s most right-wing government, and is likely to endure. Settlement construction is also likely to continue where a successor coalition sees broad political backing or a security rationale.
Gaza is the clearest test. A new government could combine military operations to defeat Hamas in the areas it still controls with diplomacy to strengthen Palestinian civilian institutions and build a credible alternative to Hamas rule.
The United Arab Emirates already participates in the Gaza Executive Board and supports the Palestinian committee established to administer Gaza. Working with the Emirates, Morocco, and other partners, a successor could help these arrangements take hold by enabling Palestinian administrators to exercise real authority.
Jewish extremist violence is another area where a new coalition could make a difference. The current government bears some of the responsibility for the violence. It has too often minimized the problem, while some ministers have given political support to extremists, despite repeated warnings from Israel’s intelligence and security services.
A coalition less dependent on National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich could end that political support and give security and law enforcement authorities stronger backing to confront the perpetrators.
That could enable a West Bank policy focused on protecting civilians, enforcing the law at agricultural settlement outposts, and reducing friction between Israelis and Palestinians.
A new government could repair Israel's standing
Lebanon and Syria offer scope for progress through security arrangements, even without formal peace.
In Lebanon, a successor could work with Washington and Beirut to consolidate the US-brokered framework signed in June. The task would be to make those commitments effective on the ground, while maintaining a hard line toward Hezbollah and demanding clear security guarantees before withdrawing from southern Lebanon.
A coalition less dependent on the far-right might have more room to pursue that goal. Hezbollah’s weakened position and continued US engagement could help, although Lebanon’s ability to enforce its commitments would remain crucial.
An agreement with Lebanon would also face fewer domestic obstacles than territorial compromise in the West Bank, with its Israeli settlements and deep historical and religious significance for many Israelis.
In Syria, a full peace agreement remains unlikely. President Ahmed al-Sharaa has reaffirmed Syria’s claim to the Golan Heights, and an Israeli government would be reluctant to relinquish territory it regards as vital to security. Syria’s civil war and October 7 have deepened that reluctance.
Even so, a successor might build on existing talks to pursue practical security understandings and expand quiet cooperation where interests overlap.
Saudi Arabia remains the biggest diplomatic prize – and one of the hardest to secure. Before October 7, Israel and Saudi Arabia appeared close to an agreement extending the Abraham Accords. Normalization has since grown more difficult.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman must weigh regional security interests against the political cost of ties with Israel, and Riyadh has explicitly linked normalization to Palestinian statehood. Shared threats from Iran and the Houthis give the two countries reasons to cooperate.
A successor would still need to determine what commitments on the Palestinian issue it could offer Riyadh. Whether the two sides could bridge that gap, and whether US President Donald Trump would invest in doing so, remains uncertain.
These openings depend in part on Israel’s standing abroad, which a new government could begin to repair. A stronger response to Jewish extremist violence and the departure of ministers such as Ben-Gvir could help restore confidence in Israel’s leadership and make international partners more receptive to its diplomatic initiatives.
That goodwill could matter most in Washington. A new government could work to rebuild support across party lines and among Americans alienated by its predecessor’s policies. The close relationship between Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has partly obscured the strain in Israel’s broader American ties.
Clearer public diplomacy, backed by substantive policy changes, could help repair them. A successor would still confront anti-Zionism and antisemitism, even as it addressed criticism of specific Israeli policies.
The next government will have little time for a honeymoon. It must seize these diplomatic openings while preserving the security Israelis demand.
The writer is a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI). In the Israeli Defense Intelligence, he served as head of the Hezbollah and Lebanon Branch (2022–2024) and later as senior adviser to the director of IDI (2024-2026).

articles.title: Golan accuses Netanyahu of coup bid after election defeat
articles.summary: Israeli opposition leader Yair Golan on Wednesday accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of attempting to overturn last week’s parliamentary election results to remain in power...
articles.full_text:
Israeli opposition leader Yair Golan on Wednesday accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of attempting to overturn last week’s parliamentary election results to remain in power despite his defeat.
Golan, who heads the Democrats party, described developments in the last 24 hours as a serious warning sign for Israeli democracy.
"Netanyahu lost. He refuses to recognize the results, and he is trying to carry out a coup and seize power by force,” Golan wrote on X.
He alleged that police arrested political activists without warrants and that the Shin Bet domestic security agency attempted to question senior elected officials without presenting evidence.
Golan also accused the outgoing government of refusing to recognize the election results, saying the developments were interconnected.
"Every additional minute that the outgoing government holds the centers of power is a danger to Israeli democracy,” he warned, urging opposition parties to form a new government as quickly as possible, restore the rule of law and prevent state institutions from being used for political purposes.
Golan also warned the heads of the police, Shin Bet and the Mossad intelligence agency: "You must be loyal to the law and the State of Israel, not to a prime minister, not to a party and not to any political interest.”
He described the situation as a security and democratic emergency, urging opposition leaders not to waste time forming a government.
The remarks came one day after Israeli opposition leaders agreed to recommend Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot to President Isaac Herzog to form the next government.
The agreement was reached during a meeting on Tuesday in Herzliya, west-central Israel, attended by Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, Golan and opposition leader Yair Lapid.
The leaders pledged to replace Netanyahu’s administration with a "national emergency government” and immediately begin drafting coalition agreements.
They also accused Netanyahu and his Likud party of conducting a campaign to undermine the legitimacy of the election results and the Central Elections Committee.
The opposition leaders agreed to coordinate parliamentary steps to replace the outgoing government and prevent another election.
Israel’s Oct. 27 parliamentary elections left Netanyahu’s bloc with 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while opposition parties secured 48 seats. The Arab parties won 19.
Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition parties independently secured the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority.
If all opposition and Arab lawmakers recommend Eisenkot, he could receive support from 67 lawmakers during Herzog’s consultations.
The opposition parties, however, have yet to agree on a governing coalition, with Lieberman ruling out participation in a minority government dependent on Arab parties.
Under Israel’s parliamentary system, the president consults elected parties before appointing a lawmaker to form a government.
The designated lawmaker initially has 28 days to form a government, with a possible extension of up to 14 days.
The government remains in office until a new administration wins the Knesset’s confidence.
The newly elected Knesset is scheduled to convene its inaugural session on Nov. 10. Opposition parties are also seeking to replace incumbent Speaker Amir Ohana of Netanyahu’s Likud party.

articles.full_text:
Elon Musk’s fortune has shrunk by more than $60 billion following Republican setbacks in the U.S. midterm elections, despite the billionaire spending an estimated $446 million to help the party maintain its grip on Congress, the Financial Times reported Wednesday.
Musk's political spending, much of it targeting the state of Texas, failed to deliver the expected results as Republicans suffered major setbacks, including in the billionaire's adopted home state.
The report said that Musk emerged as one of the biggest financial losers from Election Night, with declines in his business holdings further deepening the losses.
Tesla shares fell 5.7%, while SpaceX reportedly dropped 7.6% in early trading, adding to the pressure on Musk's fortune.
The Washington Post estimated that Musk poured $446 million into Republican campaigns, while other estimates put his political contributions at lower levels.
Much of the spending went to Senate races in Texas, where Musk-backed Republican candidates faced significant setbacks.
The election results could also complicate Musk's reported ambitions to combine Tesla and SpaceX.
A Democratic-controlled Congress may increase scrutiny of a potential merger between the two companies before President Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029. Lawmakers, however, would not necessarily have the power to block the deal.

articles.title: Who's who: Abdul El-Sayed – 1st Muslim elected to US Senate
articles.summary: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, an Egyptian American Democrat and former public health official, made history Tuesday as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate after defeating Republ...
articles.full_text:
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, an Egyptian American Democrat and former public health official, made history Tuesday as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate after defeating Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan.
The 42-year-old progressive secured the seat vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, marking a milestone for Muslim political representation in the United States.
His election followed a campaign marked by divisions within the Democratic Party, particularly over health care, economic priorities, and U.S. support for Israel.
Born in Rochester Hills, Michigan, to Egyptian immigrant parents, El-Sayed pursued a career in medicine and public health before entering politics.
He graduated from the University of Michigan in 2007, earned a doctorate in public health from the University of Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar in 2011, and received his medical degree from Columbia University in 2014.
In 2015, he became health director for Detroit, Michigan's largest city, overseeing efforts to rebuild the city's public health services following its financial crisis.
He held the position until 2017 before making an unsuccessful bid for Michigan governor in 2018, losing the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer.
El-Sayed later served as director of the Wayne County Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services from 2023 to 2025, including Detroit.
El-Sayed returned to electoral politics in 2026, defeating Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan Democratic Senate primary in August.
His campaign attracted support from prominent progressive figures, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rep. Rashida Tlaib.
He campaigned on expanding health care access through Medicare for All, lowering housing costs, reducing the influence of wealthy donors in politics and strengthening economic opportunities for working families.
On foreign policy, El-Sayed emerged as an outspoken critic of U.S. military support for Israel, describing Israel's military campaign in Gaza as genocide and calling for an end to unconditional American military assistance.
His positions on Israel became a central source of controversy during the campaign.
Stevens, whom he defeated in the Democratic primary, broke with her party just two days before the general election and endorsed Rogers, citing her concerns about El-Sayed's campaign rhetoric and political associations.
Her move drew a strong backlash among fellow Democrats but failed to derail El-Sayed's path to victory.
El-Sayed's Muslim identity also became a prominent issue during the Senate race, with President Donald Trump and other Republican figures repeatedly criticizing him for his faith and political positions.
El-Sayed rejected the attacks, arguing that the president was using his name and religion to divert attention from rising living costs and economic challenges facing Americans.
His election marks a historic first for the Senate, although Muslim Americans have previously served in the House of Representatives.
Keith Ellison became the first Muslim elected to Congress in 2006; Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar became the first Muslim women elected to Congress in 2018.

articles.title: Wind of change: US midterm elections deliver wave of historic firsts
articles.summary: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections set a series of historic firsts, with women and minority candidates breaking long-standing barriers in races for Congress and governorships. The res...
articles.full_text:
The 2026 U.S. midterm elections set a series of historic firsts, with women and minority candidates breaking long-standing barriers in races for Congress and governorships.
The results included the election of the first Black woman governor in U.S. history, the first Native American woman to win a Senate seat and the first Muslim member of Congress from New Jersey, among other milestones.
It also reshaped the balance of power in Washington. Democrats secured a majority in the U.S. Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, dealing a significant blow to the second half of President Donald Trump's presidency.
U.S. media projected a 53-42 Democratic advantage as of 7 a.m. GMT, driven by at least seven seat pickups nationwide.
Democrats also won control of the U.S. House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms after Johnny Garcia defeated Carlos De La Cruz in Texas's 35th District, according to the AP.
The victory gave Democrats the 218 seats needed for a majority in the 435-member chamber, ending Republican control and dealing a major political setback to President Donald Trump. As of 6:39 a.m. GMT, 87 seats had yet to be called.
The victories also extended beyond Washington, with Democrats winning key gubernatorial races in traditionally Republican states, including Georgia and Texas.
Abdul El-Sayed, an Egyptian American Democrat and former public health official, made history Tuesday, becoming the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate after defeating Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's closely watched midterm election.
El-Sayed, 42, is a medical doctor and former public health official who previously served as Detroit’s health director and headed the Wayne County Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services, which serves Detroit, Michigan’s largest city.
Born and raised in Michigan to an Egyptian immigrant father, he graduated from the University of Michigan, earned a doctorate from the University of Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar and received his medical degree from Columbia University.
He won the Democratic nomination in August, defeating U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in a closely watched primary. His campaign focused on health care, economic inequality and curbing corporate influence in politics.
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms made history by defeating Republican businessman Rick Jackson in Georgia, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state.
The former Atlanta mayor is also Georgia’s first woman and first Black governor. Her victory returned the governor’s office to Democrats for the first time since 1998, ending more than two decades of Republican control.
Bottoms previously served as Atlanta’s mayor from 2018 to 2022 and worked in local government before entering statewide politics.
Former U.S. Interior Secretary Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor of a U.S. state after defeating Republican Gregg Hull in New Mexico.
A citizen of the Laguna Pueblo, Haaland previously marked history in 2021 as the first Native American to serve as a U.S. Cabinet secretary when then-President Joe Biden appointed her to lead the Interior Department.
Her election marked another milestone in Native American political representation, bringing a member of an Indigenous community to state leadership.
Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate after defeating Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter.
Flanagan, an enrolled member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Tina Smith.
Before becoming lieutenant governor in 2019, she served on the Minneapolis Board of Education and represented St. Louis Park in the Minnesota House of Representatives.
She has also worked on Indigenous rights and relations between the state government and tribal nations.
Democrat Adam Hamawy won New Jersey’s 12th Congressional District, becoming the state’s first Muslim member of Congress.
A plastic surgeon and former U.S. Army combat surgeon, Hamawy defeated Republican Gregg Mele.
His election adds another milestone to the growing representation of Muslim Americans in the U.S. Congress.
Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, becoming Texas's first Latina governor.
Her victory also marked a return of Democrats to the governor’s office after more than three decades. The last Democrat to hold the post was the late Ann Richards, who left office in 1995.
Hinojosa’s win gave Democrats control of the state’s top office after years of Republican leadership and marked a significant change in Texas's political landscape.
Republican Byron Donalds became Florida’s first Black governor and the first Black Republican elected governor in U.S. history after narrowly defeating Democrat David Jolly.
Donalds, a member of the U.S. House of Representatives, will succeed Ron DeSantis. His victory also made him the first Black candidate elected to statewide office in Florida.
In Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley defeated Republican Tom Tiffany, becoming the state’s first Black governor.
Crowley previously served as Milwaukee County executive and will succeed Democrat Tony Evers.
Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, becoming Ohio’s first woman elected governor and its first Jewish governor.
A physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, Acton became widely known during the COVID-19 pandemic for her role in the state’s public health response.
Although Nancy Hollister briefly served as governor for 11 days in 1998-99, Acton is the first woman elected to the office.
Democrat Juliana Stratton’s victory in Illinois's Senate race will bring the number of Black women serving simultaneously in the chamber to three for the first time when she takes office in January 2027.
She will join Democratic Sens. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware.
Stratton, who served as Illinois lieutenant governor under Gov. J.B. Pritzker, will also become the second Black woman elected to represent Illinois in the Senate, following Carol Moseley Braun, who won her seat in 1992.
Her election means Illinois will have two people of color in the Senate, alongside Democratic Sen. Tammy Duckworth.

articles.full_text:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Wednesday that Deputy Prime Minister Carlos Cuerpo will provisionally lead the Transport Ministry following Oscar Puente’s resignation over two deadly train crashes.
Puente's resignation six days after the year's second deadly train crash left the ruling Socialists campaigning without one of their most combative, but also polarizing, voices.
In a televised address, Sanchez praised Puente for his political dignity, saying his decision helped the country regain confidence in the rail system.
Sanchez announced Cuerpo, Spain's economy minister, as Puente's replacement, saying, "Cuerpo showed a great capacity for management and integrity in this legislature."
Puente surprised lawmakers by announcing his resignation Tuesday night after four hours of intense questioning from a caretaker parliament. Most parties had demanded he take responsibility for two rail disasters that killed a combined 115 people.
One of Prime Minister Sanchez's most loyal and high-profile ministers, Puente had previously vowed to stay on to oversee the investigation into last week's crash and fix the system's flaws, despite widespread calls for his exit from both the opposition and coalition partners.
But Tuesday, the 57-year-old minister revealed he had made his decision shortly after the train crash in Urda, central Spain, only telling his family while keeping even Sanchez in the dark.
Puente's resignation takes effect once published in the official gazette. He also said he would not run in the Nov. 29 election.
Puente's surprise announcement came after polls conducted following last Wednesday's deadly crash showed a slight drop in support for the ruling Socialists. The party had hoped to campaign on its ability to uphold social services and address a housing crisis.
"Politicians like (Puente) bring honor to our country and show us that we are not all the same. While some merely preach, others give their all," Sanchez said after Puente's announcement, adding Puente had "stood up, offered solutions and then stepped aside."
A lawyer and former mayor, Puente became transport minister in Nov. 2023, overseeing the expansion of Spain's rail network and rollout of investments supported in part by EU recovery funds.
Unions and opposition parties have criticized the minister for years for underinvestment in maintenance and increased disruptions. This culminated in a Senate motion demanding his resignation in February after a fatal crash on the same Madrid-Seville line as last Wednesday's collision.
Dubbed Sanchez's "attack dog" by media commentators, he frequently traded barbs with rivals on messaging platform X or in parliament. His pugnacious style led him to become a top contender in discussions about Sanchez's eventual succession.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat Tuesday, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber and retaining a critical seat for his party.
El-Sayed’s victory in the closely contested election marked a breakthrough for the Democratic Party’s progressive wing and denied Republicans a chance to flip the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
El-Sayed, 42, a former public health official, focused on lowering costs for working families and reducing corporate influence in politics.
His platform included Medicare for All, a government-funded universal health care program championed by progressives in his party.
Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday’s midterm elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.
His opponent Mike Rogers, 63, a former congressman and FBI agent, entered the race with strong backing from Trump and national Republicans.
He had sought to cast El-Sayed as a radical candidate sympathetic to Islamic extremism through alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, claims that El-Sayed denies and that remain unsupported by evidence. Democrats said the attacks on El-Sayed relied on Islamophobic tropes.
Rogers also devoted significant effort to courting Jewish voters who may have been uneasy with El-Sayed's opposition to U.S. military aid for Israel and his condemnation of Israel's Gaza genocide.
But Rogers struggled to overcome voter concerns about the economy and Trump's low ratings. In the closing weeks of the race, he broke with the president on the war in Iran and the U.S. trade dispute with Canada, arguing that ending both was necessary to help bring down costs for businesses and consumers.
