articles.title: Democrats take Congress control in midterms sweep over Trump
articles.summary: Democrats won control of both the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives Tuesday in a nationwide rebuke of President Donald Trump that is likely to limit his ability to advance h...
articles.full_text:
Democrats won control of both the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives Tuesday in a nationwide rebuke of President Donald Trump that is likely to limit his ability to advance his agenda in his final two years in office.
The Democratic landslide will give the opposition power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump's administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments.
The results reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump's war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.
"I'm just so happy. I'm so eager," 22-year-old paralegal Michael Diaz said in Georgia, celebrating a big win by rising Democratic star Jon Ossoff in the Senate.
Trump struck a conciliatory note despite his history of questioning elections, telling The New York Times he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.
"I think the Democrats did a good job, I really do," the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. "They fought hard."
But he sought to distance himself from his own party's poor showing, adding that "I don't view it as a hit on me."
He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the defeat, while defending the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration, long one of the most divisive issues of his presidency.
As Trump was conceding, the scale of the Democratic victory grew further when former logger Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, the party's seventh Senate seat captured from Republicans.
Earlier breakthroughs in Kansas and Iowa had clinched the Senate majority for Democrats, following stunning victories in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio.
In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932. Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008.
Texas Democrat James Talarico declared he had defeated "Goliath" in winning a Senate seat while Gina Hinojosa unseated the state's Republican governor Greg Abbott, ending decades of Republican rule.
Democrats also protected key Senate seats of their own, including Ossoff in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire.
The party's House victory saw gains across Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Arizona, North Carolina and New Jersey, including districts Trump had carried comfortably in 2024.
In one closely watched bellwether, Democrat J.D. Ford ousted Republican congresswoman Victoria Spartz in Indiana, capturing a district Trump won by 17 points two years earlier.
Democrats also won Georgia's governorship, electing former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black woman governor in U.S. history.
Republicans had some consolation in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor and Ashley Moody retained a Senate seat – but only after seeing off surprisingly strong Democratic challenges.
The night was "a big wipeout and a strong repudiation of Donald Trump and his policies," George Washington University professor Todd Belt said.
Democratic control of Congress will allow the party to pursue investigations into the Iran war, immigration enforcement and allegations of corruption, while blocking Trump's legislation and senior appointments.
Robert Garcia, now expected to lead the powerful House Oversight Committee, warned Republicans on social media: "LAWYER UP."
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump's MAGA movement "on the run from sea to shining sea."
Jeffries could become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January.
Despite his conciliatory remarks, Trump also insisted on social media that Republicans would have won "IN A LANDSLIDE" if he had been running, after repeatedly urging supporters throughout the campaign to "pretend I'm on the ballot."
He also repeated his threat to use the presidential veto on Democratic-passed laws, posting a picture on social media of a red baseball cap reading just: "VETO."

Bomb threats targeted four European flights Tuesday, leading to the temporary closure of a Warsaw airport, though all planes landed safely and no explosives were found, authorities said.
Two bomb warnings targeted flights bound for Warsaw, the Polish capital, including an SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen and a LOT flight from London's Heathrow Airport.
In a third incident, Aena, the Spanish airport operator, confirmed an emergency protocol was activated following a bomb alert on a Ryanair flight from Manchester, a northwestern U.K. city, to Murcia, a city in southeastern Spain.
A Wizz Air flight from Bergamo, Italy, was inspected after landing at 9:10 a.m. GMT in Sofia, the Bulgarian capital, a Bulgarian Interior Ministry spokesperson told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The incidents followed fighter jets scrambling Monday after a Wizz Air flight from London's Luton Airport to Sofia was diverted following a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.
The Ryanair flight landed without incident Tuesday in Murcia and Spain's Civil Guard deactivated the emergency plan after checks.
Scandinavian Airlines said it could "confirm a threat against flight SK751 from Copenhagen to Warsaw."
"The aircraft landed normally in Warsaw and the passengers disembarked," it added.
Chopin Airport in Warsaw closed one runway for a security inspection of the plane, but no explosives were found.
The LOT flight, also scheduled for Chopin, diverted to Warsaw-Modlin, the Polish capital's other airport.
Authorities closed the airport following the alert, but the Boeing 737 MAX also landed safely.
"Passengers evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. No explosives were found," Adam Szablowski, a Modlin Airport spokesman, told AFP.
"The airport reopened and is operating normally," they added.
Hungary's Defense Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said Monday on Facebook that NATO's air defense alert service had issued an alert for the Wizz Air flight from Luton.
"Hungarian Defense Forces' Gripen fighter jets took to the air within minutes, ensuring the passenger aircraft's safe landing in Budapest," he said.

articles.title: 5 things you need to know about 2026 US midterm elections
articles.summary: Millions of Americans have already voted in early ballots while millions more headed for polling stations on Tuesday as the U.S. elects members of the House of Representatives, Sen...
articles.full_text:
Millions of Americans have already voted in early ballots while millions more headed for polling stations on Tuesday as the U.S. elects members of the House of Representatives, Senate and governors in states across the country.
Held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president, however, for anyone who thinks they lack drama or importance this year, consider these two statistics:
Still, midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races. More than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election, for instance.
Plenty is at stake in this midterm election as Democrats try to win majority control of the U.S. Congress.
Currently, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, where there are two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to win control.
Democrats also are fighting to win the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. They must net four additional seats to get control. Twelve races, including those in conservative-leaning states like Kansas and Texas, could decide the outcome.
Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress.
For 2026, that means that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.
The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.
Midterm election results also can give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.
Approval of Trump's performance is at a near record low of 32%, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to have an impact on the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.
At the same time, there is evidence that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans and more of them have already cast their ballots, according to the University of Florida Election Lab.
There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.
However, a landslide for the Democrats is far from assured. Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism towards Democrats, a Republican spending advantage on campaigns, and fears from moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.
Recent history tells the story of the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.
In the 2010 midterms, during the Democratic presidency of Barack Obama, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming U.S. economy and weak support for Obama's landmark health care reform legislation. Democrats lost their majority. In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.
The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time. He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.
Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House. They gained a net total of 40 House seats, but lost a net two Senate seats.
This year's elections also have races for governors in 36 of the 50 states and voting in nearly every state for seats in state-level legislative bodies.
Currently, Republicans control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.
If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker – second in line for the presidency after the vice president – is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York. He is currently the House Democratic leader.
Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to launch investigations into a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates. Jeffries repeatedly has said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.
He also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House. He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.
A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job.
Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."
Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign and an open seat in a Nebraska swing district where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the U.S. war against Iran.
Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.
Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.
Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted, falsely, that there is widespread cheating in U.S. elections. State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.

articles.title: Widening Russia-Ukraine naval war tests NATO's Black Sea limits
articles.summary: Persistent attacks in the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine are creating a major challenge for NATO in the Black Sea, leaving member states Romania and Bulgaria ex...
articles.full_text:
Persistent attacks in the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine are creating a major challenge for NATO in the Black Sea, leaving member states Romania and Bulgaria exposed.
After seven strikes on cargo ships near them, the alliance announced plans to deploy maritime patrol aircraft, drones and radar to bolster its eastern Black Sea flank.
Three days later, on Oct. 23, another ship was attacked just outside Romanian waters. Last week, naval drones sank a Greek container ship in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
Military analysts had little doubt these were Russian attacks. A naval drone in video of the last strike resembled a Russian variant, said shipping security firm Ambrey.
"I think it's undeniably an escalation," said Sidharth Kaushal, a senior fellow at the London-based RUSI think tank.
Russia denies targeting Ukraine's neighbors with drones and says European governments escalate the war in Ukraine by supplying military aid. Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
Many of the ships hit in October were near or sailing to or from a key Romanian canal used by Ukraine for exports. One was in Romanian territorial waters; eight others were in its or Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
Iulia Joja, director of the Black Sea program for the Washington-based Middle East Institute think tank, said Russia's attacks took into account the West's aversion to escalation.
"This is about testing these red lines, with full awareness that we will do everything possible to take the most minimal measures," Joja said, drawing a comparison with Russian drone incursions into NATO airspace in recent years.
A NATO official said Russian actions aimed at dissuading the allies from supporting Ukraine pose a serious security threat and the bloc's commitment to defending all its members, including those on the Black Sea, is "ironclad."
The official said there is a clear need for cost-effective counterdrone capabilities, but the alliance already committed to investing more than $40 billion in counterdrone capabilities over the next five years.
For Romania, the Black Sea is a crucial waterway for trade and home to its offshore Neptun Deep project, which will make it the European Union's largest gas producer next year. A naval drone approached Neptun Deep in August.
Bucharest has accused Russia of "systematic" strikes on civilian ships but has not attributed individual attacks, citing the need for forensic evidence. Sofia has not blamed Russia, but said some attacks appear to benefit it.
The strikes occur as Washington reassesses its military presence in Europe to focus on China. The U.S. withdrew 1,000 troops from Romania last year.
"It's a moment in the transatlantic relationship that Putin likely wants to use," a senior Romanian official said. "The EU and NATO's attention is important, and their forces currently focus on the north and the Baltics."
While NATO has reinforced its "enhanced forward presence" for the Baltics and Poland, Joja said it has not done the same in Romania despite Bucharest's requests.
"Brussels and Washington still have not decided whether the Black Sea is fully part of the NATO commitment," he added.
The Romanian official stressed Romania's pressing need for surface-to-air interceptors and radar systems to counter threats.
Joja said the limited availability of cheap interceptor weapons, exacerbated by the war in Ukraine, is a central problem for the West.
The surge in strikes on Black Sea shipping has strangled a major conduit for Russian and Ukrainian grain and oil exports.
The two sides hit 317 merchant and other vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov between May and October, more than quadrupling the 74 vessels hit in the previous half-year, according to Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey.
The tempo of attacks has fluctuated ahead of the second anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion in February. Ukraine carried out 137 attacks on ships compared with 92 Russian attacks in the third quarter, while in October, Russia hit 38 compared with five Ukrainian attacks, Ambrey said.
Ports have been damaged, and exports have shrunk, forcing Russia and Ukraine to seek alternative export routes.
Russia exported only 300,000 metric tons of grain in September through the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, down from 4.74 million metric tons in September last year, according to Russian export data reviewed by Reuters.
Ukraine suspended Black Sea port operations in late July due to Russian attacks, prompting it to divert volumes to river ports on the Danube and through Romania's Sulina Canal and its Black Sea section.
Even with this alternative route, Ukraine's port grain exports slumped to 810,000 metric tons in September compared with 2.1 million metric tons in September last year, government data show.
Andriy Ryzhenko, a naval analyst and former senior Ukrainian naval officer, said Russia's primary goal is further reducing these volumes, with testing NATO as a secondary objective.
Last week's attack occurred as the defense ministers and military chiefs of Romania, Bulgaria and fellow NATO member Türkiye met in Sofia to discuss the situation.
Türkiye's defense minister, whose country awaits responses from Moscow and Kyiv on a narrow maritime cease-fire proposal, used the meeting to warn Russia and Ukraine against further attacks.
Ankara controls the transit of warships through the Bosporus and Dardanelles under the Montreux Convention.
Several countries, including Egypt, Türkiye and India, pushed for maritime cease-fires to avert fallout from shipping disruption as global fuel and grain prices soared.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday there was growing international interest in a limited cease-fire.
Russia has rejected the idea of a narrow maritime cease-fire, saying it would provide Kyiv respite. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has sounded the alarm.
"Everyone is talking about diesel and forgetting about grain. In a month or two, everyone will start talking about an agricultural crisis," he said last month.

Africa's top health agency revised the death toll from the continent's latest Ebola outbreak to 5,376 people, most of whom died in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
According to Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) data shared Monday, 5,372 deaths occurred in Congo, with two each in Kenya and Uganda.
Congo declared its 17th Ebola outbreak in mid-May. The disease, which causes hemorrhagic fever and spreads through contact with bodily fluids, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
In the latest outbreak, 10,444 cases have been confirmed, with a fatality rate of more than 50%.
The virus has crossed borders several times in recent months. Neighboring Uganda recorded 20 cases, almost all involving people who traveled from Congo, before being declared Ebola-free in August.
In October, Kenya reported nine infections, marking its first recorded Ebola case.
That month, Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, also reported an Ebola case involving a 42-year-old Swiss woman whose husband works at the Swiss embassy in Abuja. The couple traveled to Uganda before returning to Nigeria.
The outbreak stems from the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which no approved vaccine or treatment is available.
In recent weeks, clinical trials began for the Ervebo vaccine, which proved effective against the more common Zaire strain of the virus.

Security services were verifying the threat, which reportedly affected a LOT Polish Airlines Boeing 737 MAX 8.
"At 9:54 a.m., a bomb threat alert was announced on board an aircraft operating a flight on the route London Heathrow (LHR) – Warsaw Chopin Airport (WAW). At 10:01 a.m., a Boeing 737 MAX aircraft landed at Warsaw/Modlin Airport," it said.

articles.title: Bangladesh garment workers wage protests enter 4th day
articles.summary: Bangladesh police fired tear gas Tuesday to disperse garment workers on their fourth day of wage protests, which have disrupted factories and transport in the nation's vital export...
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh police fired tear gas Tuesday to disperse garment workers on their fourth day of wage protests, which have disrupted factories and transport in the nation's vital export sector.
The unrest, which began Saturday, has intensified despite the government's move to form a six-member wage board to review pay in Bangladesh's garment sector, the world's second-largest apparel exporter after China.
This comes at a critical time for manufacturers entering the peak production season for spring and summer export orders. The industry employs about 4 million workers, supplies global brands such as H&M, Zara and Gap, and accounts for more than 80% of the country's export earnings.
Clashes were reported across industrial belts around Dhaka, including Ashulia, Gazipur and the capital's Mirpur area, as workers staged fresh demonstrations and attempted to block major highways. Dozens of people, including several police officers, were injured.
In Ashulia, police fired tear gas and sound grenades after protesters threw bricks and stones at law enforcement personnel, said Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police. Police said similar crowd-control measures were used in Dhaka's Mirpur area.
Police said additional security forces were deployed to contain the unrest. Several factories in Gazipur and Ashulia again suspended operations or declared holidays after nearly 700 factories shut a day earlier.
Workers demand a higher minimum wage of 30,000 taka ($245), up from the current 12,500 taka. They argue that rising living costs and persistent inflation have eroded their purchasing power. Several factories were also vandalized during the unrest.
Industry officials warn prolonged closures could delay shipments and damage Bangladesh's reputation as a reliable sourcing hub. It competes with rivals such as Vietnam and India for global apparel orders.
The wage dispute comes amid mounting pressure on workers from rising prices. The government formed the wage board on Nov. 1 to review pay in the garment sector, but the move has yet to calm the protests.
Factory owners said they are contending with rising operating costs, uncertainty in energy markets linked to conflict in the Middle East and softer demand in key export markets.
They warn that prolonged unrest could disrupt production schedules and jeopardize export orders, while workers continue to press for higher wages and better working conditions.

articles.title: Local truce changes little as Russia returns to pummeling Ukraine
articles.summary: Russian overnight strikes pummeled Ukraine on Tuesday, according to authorities, as renewed fighting dimmed prospects for peace in the nearly five-year war. Strikes across the coun...
articles.full_text:
Russian overnight strikes pummeled Ukraine on Tuesday, according to authorities, as renewed fighting dimmed prospects for peace in the nearly five-year war.
Strikes across the country killed dozens, forced medical facility evacuations and triggered a wave of ballistic missile alerts.
In Russia, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said air defenses destroyed nearly 500 drones heading toward the capital region.
The attacks followed a rare pause in the fighting between Russia and Ukraine in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson, which ended Sunday.
The truce, the longest of the war that began in February 2022, enabled a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Hours after the local cease-fire ended, Russia targeted a village in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, killing at least 26 people, the acting regional governor said.
Tuesday, authorities in Zaporizhzhia said Russian bombing killed 29 people.
Zaporizhzhia regional military administration head Ivan Fedorov accused Moscow of "striking people who came to receive humanitarian aid."
In the northeastern city of Kharkiv, regional military administration head Oleg Synegubov said a Russian strike hit a medical facility, wounding 25 and forcing about 200 patients to evacuate. The strike also damaged a building, its windows and nearby cars.
Ukraine's military warned of ballistic missiles heading toward Kharkiv and other parts of the country, including the capital Kyiv, Dnipro and Sumy.
Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha said a Russian strike hit critical infrastructure in Dnipro, as well as in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih.
Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday it carried out a "massive strike" on energy facilities across Ukraine and port infrastructure in the Odesa region.
Ukraine's neighbor Poland said it activated air defenses to protect its airspace, particularly in border areas.
The strikes came as Britain and France announced about 2,800 troops from 10 European countries would stage military exercises this month in support of Ukraine.
The soldiers from 10 European countries would meet in Poland for the first exercise of a new multinational force. However, the force has no offensive mission and would only be deployed once a cease-fire is agreed to end the conflict.
As the conflict entered its fifth year, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Tuesday that Washington-led talks between Russia and Ukraine would resume next week in a fresh push for diplomacy.
President Donald Trump pushed for a settlement to the war, but no breakthrough materialized.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy slammed the deadly Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia Monday, saying it hit a school distributing humanitarian aid.
"There was a moment when the next steps after the Oleshky truce could have shown progress toward peace was possible," he said.
"With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings. There must be a response to this."
Acting Regional Gov. Mykhailo Semikin said in a Telegram post that two rescue workers and four police officers were among the dead.
Last week's cease-fire, brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, enabled evacuations from Russian-occupied Oleshky to both Ukraine-controlled territory and Moscow-annexed Crimea.
A senior Ukrainian figure said Sunday that Russia refused a Ukrainian offer to extend the truce.
Ukraine's military also alleged that Moscow used the pause in fighting to "fortify its positions."
The Kremlin did not deny the accusations, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov telling reporters Monday: "This is a completely normal practice in such situations."
He alleged the Ukrainian military also used pauses in fighting in the past to regroup.
Peskov added that Moscow viewed the Oleshky humanitarian mission as "successful," praising "good cooperation between all sides" and singling out its human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, for her role.
Lantratova oversaw the cease-fire alongside her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets in one of the most substantial instances of Russian-Ukrainian cooperation since the start of the war.
The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were planned currently.
